speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF MODIFICATIONS IN GOVERNMENT PURCHASING POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on August 3,
1955,	I made an announcement with respect to the government's purchasing policy for uranium. In that announcement I stated that, while Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited, the government procurement agent, has a commitment to purchase all acceptable uranium concentrates which are offered under the published price schedule up to March 31, 1962, Eldorado has no commitment to purchase all uranium which is offered at prices higher than those contained in the published price schedule. In the circumstances, it seemed desirable that the mining industry and the public should be informed as to the future policy with respect to purchases under the special price arrangement. I stated that uranium purchased under the special price arrangement was being supplied to the United States atomic energy commission, and that there was a limit on the amount of uranium which would be so purchased. Since it was not possible for security reasons to express this limitation in terms of quantity, it was decided, as an alternative, that Eldorado would not negotiate contracts after March 31,
1956,	and that such contracts would not be negotiated unless there was satisfactory evidence that production could commence not later than April 1, 1957.
It has now been decided to modify these arrangements as follows:
Eldorado will continue to receive applications for special price contracts up to and including March 31, 1956. On or shortly after that date Eldorado will notify those applicants which are considered to be eligible for the negotiation of contracts. In making the selection of eligible applicants, the following criteria will be used. First, there must be satisfactory evidence that the applicant has an economic ore body and, second, there must be definite assurance that the property can be brought into production not later than September 30, 1957. There will be no change 67509-1104
in the present provision regarding deliveries. Deliveries under all contracts must be completed by March 31, 1962.
These modifications have been adopted because it has become quite evident in recent weeks that certain of the properties which were considered to be potential producers last August will not be able to meet the production deadline of April 1, 1957. Consequently, it is not anticipated that the total quantity of uranium which will be produced under the special price arrangement, by reason of the extension of the production deadline from April 1, 1957 to September 30, 1957, will be greatly in excess of the quantity which it was estimated might be purchased when the original production deadline of April 1, 1957, was established.
In my announcement of August 3, 1955, I also stated that the government would take under consideration the establishment of policy covering the sale of uranium which might be surplus to Canada's requirements and the commitments entered into with the United States atomic energy commission. Because of the war potential of uranium, the government must establish its export policy with due regard to security provisions. This is one of the reasons that Canada is taking an active part in the discussions of the draft statute for an international agency for atomic energy, which are now under way in Washington. It is considered advisable that any announcement as regards the establishment of export policy should await the outcome of these discussions.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I address a question to the Minister of Public Works? Has the minister now received a resolution from the city of Quebec regarding the site of the proposed post office in the constituency of Quebec

South? If so, what is the nature of the resolution and what action, if any, is contemplated by the minister?
Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Public
Works): Mr. Speaker, I have now received a letter from the city clerk of Quebec, enclosing two resolutions, both signed by the city clerk. One is a resolution of the conseil de ville and the other is a resolution of the comite administratif.
Both resolutions express objection to the site that has been chosen on Henderson street for the construction of a new postal building.
In selecting this site and developing our plans we have worked in close and friendly co-operation with the city authorities. The site has been acquired and cleared and plans are at the stage where we are ready to invite tenders for the foundation. Any change of site now would involve considerable delay and probably additional expense in getting this building under way.
I have informed the mayor that if the city council and the citizens of the city of Quebec are willing to have this project deferred, we will be prepared to receive any representations he may care to make and to participate in discussions with respect to an alternative site which it is presumed the city would arrange to make available in exchange for the one we now own and on which we are ready to build.

Therefore I will start, as I did in other years, with a short review of catch and market value and then offer the committee these short tables showing this year's catch and markets compared to last year's. In our salmon fishery on the west coast we had a disappointing year because last year was one of the low years in the four-year sockeye salmon cycle. However, that was more than compensated for by very large runs of pink salmon. The salmon situation as far as a market is concerned is a satisfactory one. As a matter of fact, the whole fish market situation at the present time is quite satisfactory. We have no surpluses, and in the case of canned salmon I believe the operators are actually allocating salmon to their customers.
The herring catch this winter on the west coast is now over 200,000 tons, one of the greatest catches in our history, and will probably finish by being the record of all time. Halibut on the west coast fell in price. A year ago we had the greatest catch in our history and that did have a softening effect on the market price. On the east coast the distinguishing activity has been the continued transition in the cod industry away from salt cod towards fresh and frozen products for the United States and Canadian markets, a very healthy development. As far as salt cod is concerned, markets are good and all stocks on hand will be disposed of by the end of the market year.
The other great fishery of the east coast is, of course, the lobster fishery. It is a very closely regulated catch but we are happy to report very high prices compared to earlier years, and that industry is in good condition. I have tables that I have put on the record in other years, first of all a weekly summary which we prepare showing prices of the principal fish in the various fishing areas and the prices of those fish a year ago. This table shows that in almost every species there is a measurable increase in price at the present time over conditions a year ago.
The second table is a summary of the landings of the principal fisheries in pounds in Canada, by species and by areas. The third table is the landed value, that is, the proceeds to the fishermen of these catches. The fourth and fifth tables describe exports to countries and the type of exports to those countries. If the committee is interested and I have their permission I should like to have these tables inserted in the record.

The domestic consumption of fish is slowly rising. I think that is due partly to the efforts of the industry and our own department to make known the advantages of fish as a food and also to the improvement both of transportation facilities and cold storage facilities across this country. Last year saw a substantial increase in the number of cold storage units which is, of course, a help to the fishing industry. Because of the condition of the industry it was not necessary to apply price support to any phase of the Canadian fishing industry last year.
On the east coast we did introduce last year a salt subsidy as a measure of encouragement to those fishermen who are engaged in the salt cod industry. It has worked out quite well and it has been, of course, of maximum aid to the fishermen in the more remote parts of the Atlantic provinces. On the west coast there is a problem which is now under consideration to improve the position of the fishermen, and that is the matter of the very great number of dogfish present in the west coast waters. These are small fish of the shark family which have a great nuisance value as predators of other fish. During wartime their livers were valuable as a source of vitamin oils. Fishermen could make money fishing dogfish just for their livers, and that kept down the number of these predators. But since the war the price of liver oil has declined because of the development of much cheaper synthetic vitamins, and on the whole it is no longer economic for the fishermen to fish dogfish in the off seasons for their livers.
A year ago the fishermen's union out west asked me whether we would pay a floor price for dogfish carcasses to be made into fish meal for which there is a reasonable market. Dogfish is not as good a source of fish meal as herring or whale, but we had an experiment conducted last year by one of the fish plants to see if dogfish could be used, and the fisheries prices support board has conducted a further study this winter. They have now assembled their information and it looks as though at least 50,000 tons of dogfish a year could be taken on the west coast in the off season. The ordinary herring reduction

plant is not quite fitted perhaps to process dogfish, but the whaling plant on the west coast and other plants, with some modifications, probably could. That matter will be discussed by the fisheries prices support board at their meeting this month.
Since we last met the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act which was passed by this parliament, has been proclaimed and the first loans have been made under it. As I predicted last year from the experience we had gained with the Farm Improvement Loans Act, the initial number of applications and approvals is small. The Farm Improvement Loans Act took at least a year or two to get really under way, but I think that the fishermen of the country are appreciative of this new source of credit through government-guaranteed loans.
Our country is one of the major fishing countries of the world, and we are particularly blessed with rich fisheries on our coasts. Some of these fisheries, lie beyond our own territorial waters, and over the years we have devised a number of very excellent international commissions to control and conserve these high-seas fisheries off our coasts. We have treaties now covering the northwest Atlantic, which includes the ten nations that fish the northwest Atlantic. We have treaties on the Pacific, the north Pacific, Japan, the United States and ourselves, and also the international salmon commission and the international halibut commission. We have the international whaling commission covering the 17 nations of the world which have whaling operations.
I think that the work of two or three of these commissions is very important this year. The first is the commission which has just been established to conserve the fisheries of the great lakes and to proceed with the extermination of the parasite sea lamprey there. Parliament approved the convention last year and we appointed our commissioners last fall. The Americans have only recently appointed their commissioners and the commission will have its first formal meeting some time late this month or early in April. We of course have not awaited the actual setting up of the commission to start work on the extermination of the lamprey. Two years ago we made our first appropriation of about $165,000. Last year we raised that to $330,000. There were a number of members from Ontario who suggested that this should be still more, but at that time I explained that money was not the limiting factor, it was our ability to secure the scientists and equipment for this lamprey control work.
We had a very good season last year in this work, and you will see in your estimates 67509-111 J
Supply-Fisheries
this year that the amount has been increased by $130,000 over last year's appropriation. We think we can find the staff to carry out extended work. There has been one interesting development during the course of the year, the development of a poison which seems to be quite effective in destroying the larvae stage of the lamprey during the four years that they are buried in the mud. If that works out successfully it will speed up a great deal our program for the extermination of the lamprey. All Ontario members from the great lakes area have been keen on this but the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) has spoken about it on several occasions. Actually he is away today with our films and our lamprey specimens addressing a game club on this problem. As a result of that, when we come to item 152 I propose to have it stand until some time later in the month when he will be here so he can speak on it.
The next commission in which hon. members have a special interest this year is the international Pacific salmon commission. This commission was formed by Canada and the United States and controls the great sockeye fishery of the Fraser river. This is the weakest year of the four-year cycle of the sockeye salmon, and as a consequence the salmon commission, at their recent meeting on the west coast, approved the most stringent control regulations which they have yet asked us to implement. They point out that not only is this the weakest of the four-year cycle years, but they also point to the very great improvement in the fishing efficiency of both the Canadian and United States salmon fleet, with the most modern of boats, nylon nets, drum seines, power blocks and all these other improvements.
One of the proposals made by the salmon commission, and one which was mentioned in a question earlier this session by the hon.
member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Pearkes), was the proposal that all fishing be stopped in outside Canadian waters. It is only in recent years that we have actually begun to fish those waters. Before the sockeye would swing around the end of Vancouver island into the strait of Juan de Fuca, where the United States fishermen would get their half of the fish. The sockeye would then go into the gulf of Georgia and up the Fraser river where our fishermen would get their half of the fish. In recent years, especially since the last war, we have encouraged the fishermen to get out to sea and establish historic rights on the high sea fishery, and also to put us in a little better position. In the past, we got the second half of the fish.

The salmon commission has been extraordinarily successful in dividing the catch. I think there was a difference of less than a fraction of one per cent over the last 10 years. Nevertheless, we were always in a position of getting the second half of the fish. I though it would be much better if we had the first crack, then the United States got their share and we topped off by fishing in the second Canadian water. So far as the other four species of salmon are concerned, which are not covered by this commission, the outside fishing is most important. Unless we fish out there the United States fishermen get the first crack at these fish as they pass Puget sound on their way to the Fraser river. It was for that reason that two years ago I encouraged the fishing industry to bring in 15 big deep sea seiners so we could build up our share of this fishery in outside waters. It is for this reason that the suggested closing of these waters is of particular importance to the Canadian fishing industry.
This proposal, I am informed by my legal advisers, is in direct contravention of the commission treaty which was approved by this house in 1937. Article 4 of the treaty says that if any of the Canadian waters are to be closed, all the Canadian waters are to be closed; if any of the United States waters are to be closed, all the United States waters are to be closed. It is quite true that over the years there may have been minor variations in that we did agree upon closing inside areas for week end closures of different lengths, but never have we agreed, in violation of the treaty, to a complete closure of a very important Canadian fishing area. I have, therefore, written the chairman of the international commission telling him, first of all, that this is in contravention of the treaty approved by this parliament, and while I have the power as Minister of Fisheries under the Fisheries Act to order such a closure, I was not given the power by this parliament to exercise it under the terms of the international Pacific salmon convention. I have asked him, therefore, to reconsider the proposal and see whether the same conservation results can be achieved without this precedent of completely closing an important Canadian area, an area which is of very great importance to us in other fisheries as well as in the sockeye salmon fishery at the moment.
I told the chairman that the Canadian people are most appreciative of the magnificent job the commission has done in reestablishing this great fishery. I said that if, over the years the commission has found from its experience that certain articles of the convention are hampering its work, then we in this parliament certainly would be

very glad to hear its recommendation for change, and that would be the proper way to do it.
One other important issue in connection with the Fraser river is this matter of fish and power. The Fraser river salmon fishery is the most important single fishery in Canada. It is the greatest single salmon fishery in the world. The landed value and the market value of this one fishery exceeds the landed and market value of all the cod, for example, on the east coast or of all the lobsters on the east coast. It has been saved, as I said, by the very wise management of these scientists and the administrators of the international salmon commission. The present average market value is about $25 million. The salmon commission feels quite confident that within the foreseeable future they can double that to $50 million a year. Of course, that is welcome news to the fishing industry of British Columbia.
On the other hand our province-when I say "our province" I am of course a British Columbia member-is growing at an extraordinary rate, especially in the development of industry. Industry in this country is always hungry for power. In British Columbia we have both public power and private power and those agencies have, since the war, engaged in a great program of expansion. I think, for example, that our province was the only province which did not have brownouts or blackouts because our public and private power agencies were able to keep ahead of the times.
Now the point has been reached when they are beginning to look towards the Fraser river in their search for more sources of power. This, of course, has alarmed the fishing industry. There are two general proposals. One is that 10 low level dams could be constructed, four on the lower Fraser and six on the Thompson, which would be capable of a very large production of power but which, in the opinion of the fishing industry, would do practically irreparable damage to that industry. The other suggestion is for one very high level dam, a dam of over 700 feet, on the main stem of the Fraser. The position taken by the fishing industry and the Department of Fisheries on this matter is a very simple one. We feel, first of all, that every non-salmon stream in the province should be developed for power before a salmon stream is touched. In that respect we feel that, before the Fraser is touched, that part of the Columbia river in Canada should be exploited to the full. At one time the Columbia was a great salmon stream but the construction in the United States of six big dams impaired the fishery and the construction of the enormous Grand Coulee dam

ended all movement of salmon above that dam into Canadian waters.
At Mica creek on the Columbia there is a possibility of tremendous power developments. A year ago some power people were saying that Mica creek was too far from Vancouver and Victoria, from the industrial area of British Columbia, to be economically possible. Last summer on my way to Russia I stopped off at Norway and Sweden to see the fisheries people there, and I was especially interested to find that in Sweden they ship power 600 miles from northern Sweden down to the industrial area around Stockholm. The distance from Mica creek to Vancouver is around 300 miles. It is true they use different techniques in Sweden, very high voltage, 800,000 volts, and a different type of conductor, bundle conductors; but there is no reason why exactly the same technique should not be used in British Columbia to bring Columbia power into the Vancouver area.
The second position of the fishing industry in British Columbia and of our department is that even when the known salmon streams are exhausted there should be no dams built on the Fraser until we have discovered how we can safely pass the adult salmon over the dam on the way to the spawning ground and the more difficult thing of passing the salmon fingerlings down over the dam on the way to the sea. Since this is probably the most important fishing problem which we are going to be confronted with in Canada for the next two or three years, I would like to take a moment or two to tell hon. members from other parts of Canada the essence of the problem.
The five species of west coast salmon, as they enter the river to spawn, stop feeding. Unlike the Atlantic salmon, when they have spawned they die in the river they do not return to the sea. And so these salmon enter the streams in tremendous numbers with this as yet unexplained blind instinct which brings them up back to the little creek in which they themselves were spawned two, four or five years before to spawn and to die.
The sockeye salmon, our most valuable salmon, is the one in which that homing instinct is most developed. It is also the salmon which goes the farthest. Some of these salmon go 700 miles up the tributaries of that great river to find their spawning grounds. These fish live off their bodies during this long and difficult passage, and any delay by a dam or by any other obstacle, by a natural obstacle of a falls or by high water making the speed so great that the salmon cannot breast it, any delay like that means that the salmon has not got enough energy
Supply-Fisheries
stored in his body to get to the spawning ground in time to spawn. Each of these series of ten dams of course means ten delays, which in this case would result in the greatest of all salmon runs, the Adams river run, a small tributary of the Fraser, being met with these ten delays.
The actual passage of adult fish up over dams is not too difficult. We have had this problem for quite a number of years on both coasts. Dams are getting higher and higher but it is still possible to bring them up. There is another problem which arises, and that is the difference in water temperatures. Instead of having an even flow in the river you have these great storages of water with a limited spill over the dams at certain times; therefore, there is a change in water temperature.
One of the ways in which the salmon does find its way is by constantly breasting the current. Some of these dams will create enormous lakes behind the dams, so even when the adult salmon is up over the dam he is then at a loss. Instead of breasting the strong stream and forging his way on he is lost in a lake in which there is very little current. The other point, of course, is that these great lakes formed behind dams raise the water level in the lower stretch of the flooded area and cover spawning grounds which have been used by the salmon in the past.
As far as the fingerlings are concerned, they of course move in very much greater numbers. They have a much more difficult time. They can either go over the top of the dam or go through the turbines. If they go over the top of the dam damage is done in two ways. Either the fingerling touching the concrete face of the dam gets its very tender skin abraded off, or it dies of shock as it hits the pool at the bottom.
The turbine is another hazard, as one could well expect. The penstocks drawing the water for the turbines will suck the small fish down. They sustain the first damage as they pass through the whirling blades of the turbine as they go through. Much the greater damage, however, is done through the tremendous changes in pressure on the sides of the turbine. A 100-foot penstock has a water pressure of 45 pounds per square inch. On this side the fish is whirled through suddenly, and there is no pressure other than air pressure on the other side. It is like the way in which they make puffed wheat. They put grain under great steam pressure and suddenly release it and the wheat blows out in a puffed form. When that happens to the little finger-ling it ruptures the blood vessels and the fingerling dies.
What have we done to study these problems? Our own department has been working

on this problem almost since it was formed. Scientific research has been working on it pretty constantly since 1921. On the United States side the state of Washington, of course, was the most concerned. The United States army engineers have done work on the dams on the Columbia on the United States side. In Norway and in Scotland, where they have runs of Atlantic salmon, they have done quite a bit of work on this, but their problem is very different from ours in that they are dealing with fish whose numbers are in the hundreds and we are dealing with fish whose numbers are in the millions.
Last summer, in Russia, after the whaling commission meetings were over my main interest in getting to Siberia was to see what the Russians had done on this problem. We have not been able to have very much of an exchange of scientific documents with them until the last four or five months, but we knew they had the same problem because they have a great Pacific fishery, of the same types of salmon as we have, along the shores of Siberia, in the Amur river, and Kamchatka. We knew that they had done a great deal of work on electrical fishing, using electricity as a means of fishing, and of electrical pumps for the transportation of fish. But when I got up there I found that part of Siberia still almost a virgin wilderness. There is very little industrial development there, and in the first 1,500 miles of the Amur river there is not a single dam. In the sea of Okhotsk and Kamchatka fisheries there are no dams at all; therefore, the Russians have not had to grapple with this problem yet. In some of their western rivers, the Volga and the Don, they do have the problem of moving up sturgeon and other river fish around their power developments. It is a very different problem because these fish live in the river and feed in the river, so are not destroyed by delays. Their number is small and they are slow-moving fish.
Well, in the last 30 years our department has solved these dam problems as they came up by building fishways and by building fish ladders. The highest dam built so far in British Columbia on a salmon stream is in the Capilano river in my riding, a 350 foot dam. It is too high for any fishway that we had knowledge of. So there we actually trap the fish at the foot of the dam and take them around in tank cars, several miles around the dam, to where the stream enters the back of the lake above the dam, so they can start on their way again. But the problem in the Fraser is a much greater one. In the Capilano, for example, they move about 6,000 fish a day that way. At Bonneville dam on the Columbia the United States

army engineers have devised a means which can carry a maximum of 200,000 fish a day. But to get salmon in the Fraser to the head of the spawning streams, our facilities will have to carry at least 750,000 fish a day on the lower Fraser and above the junction of the Thompson half a million in the Thompson, and a quarter of a million a day on the upper main stem of the Fraser.
In the last few years the salmon commission and the two departments of fisheries of Canada and of the state of Washington have conducted a lot of practical experiments. At one high dam, the Baker dam in the state of Washington, a dam of about 100 feet, we found that 70 per cent of the fingerlings going over the top were killed, and 30 per cent of the fingerlings going through the turbines were killed. But over and above that there is a mortality of the fingerlings who survived either the great drop over the dams or the passage through the turbines because, although they are still living when they have got through, they have been damaged and they are not as lively as if they had not had that experience. Because of that they undoubtedly fall prey much more easily to predators in the river, the trout, or the predators in the sea, and therefore the losses are probably even higher than that.
We have done a great deal of work in the matter of the diversion of the fingerlings before they reach the dam. The numbers are probably 50 times as great as the adult salmon going up. As far as the spillways are concerned, we insist on these dams on salmon streams having a smooth surface on the spillway face so abrasion is cut to a minimum. Instead of having the fish hurled down into the pools, all the new dams have a lip at the foot like a ski-jump, so the fish are carried up in a spray before dropping into the pool at the base.
On the Capilano dam we do more than that. We had a serrated edge put into the base so the ski-jump effect goes off in different levels, but even then the mortality is still high. As far as the penstocks are concerned, that can be solved with very high dams. The fingerlings are mostly in the top 100 feet of the river or lake and are very seldom below 200 feet, so if you put the turbine penstocks more than 200 feet down the fingerlings will not be drawn through the turbines.
On our rivers, we have tried in many ways to divert the fingerlings just as they come down the stream before entering the pool above the dam. We have tried screens and light, we have tried air bubbles, we have tried electrical impulses, we have tried electrical fields and we have tried a curtain of chain

'which seems to be the best at the moment. We have also tried scent, both the scent of seals and human scent from which the little fish are instinctively turned away, and we have also tried colours. Some of these things have been quite successful in the lab but when you transfer these experiments from the lab to a river such as the Fraser, none of these things are strong enough to withstand the surging current carrying logs and roots which sweep away any type of barrier.
Another problem is to divert enough water to the sides of the lake to carry the finger-lings. There are proposed 10 dams of less than 100 feet in the Fraser. Our officials say this means the end of the salmon run in this part of the river. There will be ten delays on the fish getting up to the Adams river, for example. If the mortality of fingerlings coming downstream is just 50 per cent for each dam, that mortality is a geometric progression. With ten dams and a 50 per cent mortality it means you have a one thousand and twenty fourth part of your fingerling salmon at the end of the last dam, and that ends the fishery. These dams would have to handle five species of salmon and these species have different migration periods. Since the dams are all less than 100 feet we will have a mortality from suction through the turbines as well as death from going over the top of the dams.
I understand that the power company most interested in the Fraser now proposes to build just one low level dam on the Fraser which will carry them along until such time as the Columbia power can be brought down.
The Moran dam is a very different problem. It will be one of the highest in the world, over 700 feet high. There will be no penstock trouble because they can be situated below where the fingerlings are. The problem is how to get the migrant fingerlings down the 700 foot drop. The engineers are suggesting a lip just below the spillway to divert the fish down the side by tubes, but it will take a long gradient, otherwise the fish will go down just the same as over the top.
The other difficulty at the Moran dam is the enormous lake which will be created behind it. I have read it will be 164 miles long, so the salmon which gets over the dam instead of encountering the river current will be lost in the lack of current in an enormous lake. This lake will also mean the flooding of many spawning beds.
What are we doing about it? We are stepping up our research program on fish migration. Mr. H. R. MacMillan, one of the members of the salmon commission, gave a grant of more than $100,000 to the fisheries institute
Supply-Fisheries
of the University of British Columbia for research and the British Columbia electrical power company, one of the companies involved, has given a grant of $50,000 to the university. These grants to the university will of course enable them to do more research but much of the research has already been done by the fishery scientists of the salmon commission and the department. What the university will be able to do will be to assemble all known data on this problem of the movement of fish over dams, and place it before the proper authorities.

I have only one little piece left. I was going to say that the other thing which makes the situation easier is the very harmonious relations there have been between industry and the fishing groups in British Columbia over the years. Up until now we have been able to have fish and power in British Columbia and the attitude of the British Columbia Electric Company in making money available to study this problem is an example of that kind of feeling. The provincial government has also been most helpful. They have announced that no licences will be granted on the Fraser river for a power dam until the problem of the movement of fish has been solved.
I was going to raise the matter of one other international commission which is probably the one which has always intrigued hon. members the most. I refer to the fur seal convention to cover the fur seals of the Pribilof islands. Originally there were four nations participating, Japan, Russia, Canada and the United States, which had agreed to end the high seas hunting of these seals and keep a reserve to restore them. Japan and Russia dropped out and the United States and Canada have carried on alone for the last 15 years. There has been a great achievement in the restoration of the species which in 1911 seemed to be on the point of extinction. Our problem now is that fishermen say there are too many fur seals which destroy fish which they use as food. We get one-fifth of the kill on the Pribilof islands in return for abstaining from killing them off the coast of British Columbia. Last year our receipts from that were $1,214,331, about $200,000 more than the previous year. The

Supply-Fisheries
average price received for the skins was $94.80. The Japanese and Russian fishermen in recent years have also been unhappy about the number of fur seals in the north Pacific
and so a meeting was convened in Washington last December to see if we could arrive at a new four-power treaty to solve this problem. Seals of course are animals and this is not a true fishery matter, but it is an interesting industry.
Negotiations have proceeded very slowly but we hope that in the end we will have a treaty which will be acceptable to us, by which we will have a closer control over the numbers and which will still return to us about $1 million a year.
I thank the house for giving me these few extra minutes. I shall simply close by saying that generally the fishing industry is in pretty good condition. As I said last year, fishing is still probably the most dangerous and the most ill-paid occupation in Canada, but to the men engaged in the industry it is more than that. It is a way of life, and as long as the fishing industry is a little better this year than the previous year' the fishermen are reasonably happy and like other fishermen, either sport or commercial fishermen, they are always optimistic that the next catch is going to be the big one.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that those of us who have listened to the minister's opening statement this morning, as on similar occasions, have been pleased with the casual and yet interesting and almost dramatic way in which he deals with some of the phases and activities of his department.
I am quite sure when the time comes for the minister to retire from public life he need not worry about his opportunity to earn a living because he will certainly be able to write novels about the sea from which he will probably earn far more money than he earns today.
I want to say most sincerely that the minister makes his department most interesting. Possibly there are very few departments in the government where that opportunity is presented, which may be one explanation. As the minister said in his concluding remarks, this is a way of life for many people. It is a hard way of life. I think all people who know the fishermen-this certainly applies on the east coast-will agree that they are among the poorest paid for the hardest work of people engaged in any occupation in Canada today. Yet few of them would change. They love the life and have developed a type of citizenship and outlook which permits them to make a contribution which is well worth while.
,
Taking it in all, I submit that this department warrants more interest than has been shown in the past. It may be merely a coincidence or an accident, but I am certainly glad to see the estimates of this department being brought down at this relatively early stage in the session. Back over the years I have found that the fisheries estimates have been brought down in the latter part of the sessions. Last year I think they were brought down on June 24 or 25, and the same with other years. It is good to see that we are to be given a little more time in which to consider these matters and I think also to emphasize the position of this department in the economy of Canada rather than to have these estimates considered as being something to be got on with whenever it was convenient, more particularly when the weather was hot and we might not be ready to spend so much time talking about these matters.
Perhaps I should say at this point how delighted we all are to see the minister back again apparently restored to health. We were all shocked and I think I can say frankly worried at the reports we heard of his accident and consequent injuries. It is good to see him in his present shape. I am sure that if during these estimates he finds he is being asked too many questions or is being bothered in any way we will be only too glad to have him remain seated. I would hope that before we finish with his estimates the minister will find it possible to refer to what he saw in the Scandinavian countries and even in Russia and to make a comparison between their methods of fishing and industrial production with our own.
Before I was diverted to making a personal reference, I was saying that this is a most important industry. There are all these people engaged on the east and west coasts, in the central part of Canada and the great lakes, and in the north on Great Slave lake and others. I profess to have no knowledge whatsoever of the fishing industry except in a most casual way and that only with reference to the east coast. As the minister has said, the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) has taken particular interest in the fisheries of the great lakes. I was glad to hear the minister say that if this particular item were reached it would be allowed to stand until that hon. member was present. There are other hon. members from Ontario who no doubt will be speaking today, and there are also members from the west coast who will be dealing with the fisheries on the Pacific.
I checked yesterday to find the relative value of the production of this industry as

compared with other industries in Canada. The 1955 figures for other industries are not available as yet, so I took the 1954 figures. As the minister said this morning, the landed value of fish for 1954 was $86 million. That is not a tremendous amount, but it is fairly substantial. The 1954 market value, which is a fair criterion, and which would be the value of the product when frozen, processed and ready to move from the plant, not the retail value, was almost $192 million for 1954.
We hear a great deal about the tobacco industry in this country, but it might be interesting to note that the production of that industry for 1954 was just about one-quarter of the market value of our fisheries. We hear a great deal about our farm implement industry and the tremendous exports of farm implements, but the total 1954 production of that industry was $113 million as compared with $192 million for our fisheries. Even the gigantic motor car industry showed only a total production value of $559 million, or roughly two and a half times the market value of our fisheries. I could go on and make other comparisons, but I bring forward these figures in order to bring this industry into a clearer focus than it has been in the past.
I submit that this industry deserves more careful attention and consideration than it has always received in the past. It is a unique industry. During the past few weeks we have heard a great deal of discussion in the house about wheat, and the production of other crops has been discussed, which is proper and right, but this industry is unique in that there is no ownership in it at all. Not only is it public domain, but it is a watery public domain and no one has any vested interests in it, except in so far as territorial waters are concerned.
I sometimes wonder that people have the courage to spend substantial sums of money developing plant and investing in equipment without any assurance that the industry will be protected and with the possibility that nationals of other countries or even our own nationals who are not to well controlled may come in and destroy the very basis of the industry. As I say, in that respect it is a unique industry.
As the minister said, there are two basic problems confronting the industry, the problem of marketing and the problem of conservation. As he said also, the problem of marketing seems to be a little better this year. At least we do not have to have floor prices. As the minister has said, the surpluses are going to be disposed of and from that standpoint the industry is in better shape than it has been in prior years.
Supply-Fisheries
I think a great deal of credit should go to the economics and marketing divisions of the department. Personally I rather regretted a reduction in these items. It is true the reduction is not large, but I submit that more money should be provided for the marketing and economics divisions of this department. Those activities should be stressed.
The fact is that we still eat too little fish in this country. Not enough emphasis has been placed on the eating of fish. The minister has indicated that the industry is cooperating in an advertising campaign. I think the industry should be encouraged to spend more money on advertising and the department should be prepared to co-operate by supplementing that advertising. Better packaging, improved curing methods, faster freezing methods and quicker transportation have increased the demand for fish. The people of Canada should be encouraged to eat more fish, and I am thinking of the Nova Scotian finnan haddie that we have from time to time in the parliamentary restaurant. If more people knew of that product the consumption would increase tremendously. I suggest that you cannot find a better cured fish anywhere in the world. That is just one example of the improvement which has been going on consistently in this industry.
Because of these improved methods and because our population is increasing and will continue to increase, we hope fairly rapidly, there is no doubt that the demand for fish will increase as well. I think this demand could be spurred if there were more direct assistance from the marketing branch than has been the case heretofore.
Then there is the problem of our exports. I am speaking now purely for the east coast where our exports other than to the United States and forgetting for the moment lobsters and a few special products such as that, take the form of cured and salted fish.
The minister has said in other years that that was a very uneconomic way of disposing of this, and that of course the emphasis should be laid on the development of the fresh fish consumption. That is true, but, after all, we have to have the cured fish outlet in order to take care of surpluses, because fish is not a product which can be stored indefinitely. There has to be a cured fish market. I know that many fishermen in my own constituency, perhaps carrying on in a small way, when they find that fresh fish sells for only 1| cents a pound, do the curing themselves and hold it until the fall when they can get a much higher price than on the fresh fish market. Therefore I do not think we should overlook the importance of

Supply-Fisheries
maintaining and developing the market for our salted and cured fish. At one time that was the principal one, of course. There was an extensive market in Spain and other parts of Europe, in the Caribbean, in South American countries and so on. That has been widely restricted today. The demand is less today, but there is still a substantial demand in the Caribbean. I noticed the other day that the republic of Haiti have sent a trade delegation here to negotiate or discuss the possibility of amplified trade arrangements between our two countries. When we entered the British West Indies trade agreement in the early 1920's, it was undoubtedly a good thing, but I think it did create prejudices and frictions with other Caribbean countries which were at that time buying tremendous quantities of our salted and cured fish. I urge on the minister that he lose no oportunity whatsoever in attempting to develop in every way possible those other markets in the Caribbean and in South America in those products.
Of course, the trouble down there is that for the most part those people have a very low purchasing power. They are among the poorest paid in the world and they cannot afford to buy an expensive product. We shall have to have manufacturing and processing carried on in this country so that we can afford to put those products in those markets at prices at which those people can buy them. If that is done-and I believe it can be done-and the industry restored to some extent to what it was many years ago, it certainly will be of assistance to those of us who represent the fishing industry in the eastern part of Canada. I shall say nothing more about marketing at the moment. There will undoubtedly be much more said about that subject as the day goes on, but I simply say again that this Caribbean market is a traditional market for the Atlantic provinces. I am not minimizing the fresh fish trade. Gradually, as fresh fish production is improved more and more, that market will perhaps play a less and less important part in our economy, but it still is an important factor and should not be overlooked.
The matter of conservation, to which the minister referred, is the other important phase of the department to which we all have to give a great deal of attention. We have the bifocal problem, shall we say, of our territorial waters and the high seas. In the territorial waters there should be no problem. We have control of those waters. We make the regulations, and it is simply a matter of enforcing them. The responsibility for that is our own. But when we get beyond those territorial waters on to the high
[Mr. Nowlan.l
seas, there you get the problem in its very essence, and today it is, I think, a pressing problem.
Think of the changes that have taken place in the methods of fishing in the past few years. Almost all of us in this chamber have memories of the times when fishing was carried on by means of the schooner and the dory. That was the method that had been carried on for 500 years. When the Portuguese said last year that they had been fishing on the banks for 500 years, that was true historically. That was the method that had been employed. Then came the evolution from the schooners to the great voracious trawlers. In a lucky day, I should say, a trawler would haul out as much fish as a schooner would get in a month. In the old days, of course, we had the hardy men of the sea, such as the Minister of Public Works has in his constituency, going out in the fishing schooners, the Bluenose and the other champion craft which were built for the international competitions. That day, unfortunately, is gone. That was part of the colour and the drama, and it went with the coming of the mechanical trawler. With the mechanical trawler has come a greater threat to the fish as a whole, because today you have the trawler with its trawls and its equipment-with the most modern electronic equipment with sounding devices enabling them to move along, as I understand it, and pick out very accurately where the schools of fish are located. There are also, of course, ship-to-shore telephone communications, by means of which they can receive instructions from hour to hour as to their movements. Altogether, although the banks are very large and the fish, you might say, are very small, their chances of avoiding those trawlers today are getting less and less as the days go by. It has become a highly scientific and technical procedure, though still very dangerous and rough on the men taking part. As a result of all this-and when you remember that there are more ships on the banks today from other countries than there are from Canada, that they come in there from Portugal and other parts of Europe, from the United States and from all over the world-you might say that fishing in that area, with these modern devices and equipment, has made the necessity for conservation even greater now than it ever was before.
The minister says, quite properly, that the only way you can deal with this is by international conventions. We are very happy to have made great progress along the lines of international conventions within the past few years, but they move painfully slowly, as the minister indicated almost as

an aside in what he told us about one of the great lakes commissions, when he said that only in the past three or four weeks one of the contracting parties had found time to appoint personnel to that commission.
I was just reminded of the province of Nova Scotia, a small province. I wonder how many hon. members outside the fishing industry realize that the average landed catch for that province within the past two or three years has been in the neighbourhood of 375 million pounds of fish per year. That is over one million pounds of fish a day, on the average, being brought in to the wharves of that one province. When you amplify the picture by considering all the fishing countries in the world that are searching for and catching fish over the areas of the banks today, I suggest to you that the time has come when a much more radical approach must be made to the problem. I know the minister is hoping that through the commissions there can be evolved regulations that can conserve the fish, and it must be done.
Yesterday, in reading a report of his department, one of the research bulletins, I was struck with the fact that when the lobster fishermen first began catching lobsters in the maritime provinces and the province of Quebec almost 100 years ago, that lobster fishery developed in a few years, so that 75 years ago they were catching over one hundred millions pounds of lobsters a year. Of course, they were large and heavy lobsters. From that the fishery dropped to approximately 20 million pounds. Now, through conservation and control, it has been kept roughly in balance between catch and production and we are at around 35 million pounds again. I think that is approximately the situation. It shows what conservation can do and it also shows what will happen, that there is a rapid fall if there is no conservation. So I say that we need to put more emphasis on that.
These waters are at our front door. One does not want to become provincial, one does not want to become perhaps supernationalist, but we have a greater interest in them than any other country in the world and they are being exploited by all the countries of the world. I think the time has come when our government will have to take more stringent steps and make a firmer approach to the matter than has been the case in the past. It is going to be slow, it is going to be laborious, it is going to be tedious. You are going to be stymied by one country after another which wishes to avoid being involved in too stringent regulations. However, as I have said, I think the time has come when
Supply-Fisheries
there must be more emphasis put on the matter than there has been in the past. I know that the minister entirely approves but he of course is faced with the difficulties of international negotiation and the slow tedious process of dealing with commissions. Besides, he has many other things to do.
But we can easily get disease or pestilence in our fish. Take what happened last summer with the herring when suddenly overnight hundreds of thousands of herring were found dying in the waters because of some disease or pestilence that had struck and which virtually extinguished them. At the same time, of course, pollution was created in the waters which made the life cycle of other fish much more difficult. There again there is a necessity for such action.
As I said, there are two approaches to the matter. One is the international approach which the minister suggested and urged and which I suggest he pursue still further. Then there is also the approach of control of our own waters. I know the minister can say that he knows exactly what I will say because I said it last year. In fact the discouraging thing about it is that last night I looked up what I said last year and I thought I could almost say the same thing over again word for word. It is rather discouraging but nevertheless I think it is important because the problem of our territorial waters is an important one to many members and I think to the country as a whole.
I am not going to weary the house by repeating things I have said before on this phase of it so far as my own constituency is concerned. Perhaps when the specific items are before us later today I will elaborate on the matter a bit. But you have the situation where under the old law that exists today international law recognizes the three-mile limit as territorial water. Historically, of course, that is based on the old theory of the cannon shot. History tells us that the old cannons could fire three miles out from shore. Therefore you could exercise control over those waters and beyond that was the high seas. If that theory was sound then, it has certainly got to be reviewed today in the light of present developments. Where you would apply the limit no one of course knows because today it is not a question of three miles. With a bomber I suppose it is 3,000 miles or with an intercontinental ballistic missile it might be 5,000 miles.
No one wants to suggest extremes such as those, but there are those who have suggested 10, 12 or 20 miles. I understand that some South American countries extended the limit last year to 200 miles, and altogether

Supply-Fisheries
the situation is most uncertain. I believe the question was referred to the international law committee of the United Nations, and last year the minister told us that the committee was about to report and that the United Nations would take some action thereon. But we know how dreadfully slow and tedious any action on the part of the United Nations can be.
The minister also told us last year that an interdepartmental committee had been set up of which Dean Curtis formerly of Dal-housie law school was either the chairman or the technical advisor. I have forgotten which. Dalhousie law school is of course where he really got his educational foundation although he may have moved away temporarily to the University of British Columbia.
We will not debate that, Mr. Chairman. I know where he got his training in the days before he was exposed to the vagaries of British Columbia.
What I want to say, and I realize that my time is running out, is that the minister told us last year when I mentioned this matter that Dean Curtis' report had been submitted to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and that he understood that after the government had considered it it would be made available to parliament. That was a year ago. Perhaps I should not say a year ago because this year the estimates are before us earlier, but it is nine months ago and I am sure that the government has had time to consider the report. I should like the minister to tell us if he will make the report available to parliament because I think it is a most important thing.
We need to know what the policy of our government is with respect to international control of our own territorial waters. Before the estimates are through I think the minister should clarify the position with respect to the report of the interdepartmental committee and also what position the representatives of the government are prepared to take when the matter is considered further by the United Nations this fall. Certainly the time has come when the whole set-up must be reviewed. I could make references to my own constituency but I am not going to do so because, Mr. Chairman, I see that you are looking apprehensively at the clock.
But we have this situation with respect to trawlers. The minister knows it and the anomaly of the problem must irritate him more than anything else. I presume that sometimes he feels frustrated and helpless about it and would like to throw the problem out the window. I suggest that he throw the 
trawlers out the window. Of course, from the standpoint of my constituency that would be a delightful way of solving the problem. However, as the committee has been told before, under international law any United States trawler can come up to within three miles of our coastline. When I say "within", that is really euphemism, because in a fog the three miles becomes constricted to about 30 yards if the water is deep enough. All the fishermen in my constituency can certify that is so because of the lobster traps, trawls and everything else that they lose to some of these American trawlers. Despite their sonic equipment and everything else they suddenly become lost and wander up along the coast. On the other hand, Canadian trawlers over 65 feet long, manned by Canadian crews and built with Canadian money, are required to stay outside the 12-mile limit which I think is the rational approach to the matter. If the minister will say that we are going to have a 12-mile limit, our government is going to insist on that limit and we are going to take that position with the United States right away and we are going to urge a 12-mile limit before the United Nations, I think it would clarify the air.
But at the moment you have that conflict between international law and our own internal regulations. No wonder everyone is frustrated and angry about it. Certainly Canadian trawlers feel they have the right to go up to the 3-mile limit if the Americans are allowed to do so. On the other hand, the inshore fishermen do not want to see the trawlers nearer the coast than they can help. I should like to see the situation worked out so that all trawlers would be kept 12 miles off our coasts. That would protect the inshore fishermen who perhaps are not the most important in this industry from an economic point of view but still have that way of life to which the minister referred. There are scores and scores of villages and thousands of people involved, some of them,
I presume, in the constituency of my friend, the hon. member for Charlotte, some in the constituency of Saint John-Albert in New Brunswick on the other side of the bay, and all up and down the coast of my constituency of Digby-Annapolis-Kings.
Of course the minister has power with respect to this matter. You may remember that I twitted him a bit a year ago in that he had taken unto himself the power to draw a line in St. Margaret's bay and say thus far shall you go and no farther. He barred the trawlers from crossing that line. Of course, that happened to be just before the last provincial election.

speechtext: Pure coincidence.

That year it was a coincidence. By another coincidence there is another provincial election in Nova Scotia this year, and I think it would be a fortunate coincidence if he would make the same ruling with respect to the coastline of the bay of Fundy as he did three years ago with respect to St. Margaret's bay and say that all trawlers, big or small, must keep outside that line. That would not only be a coincidence but it might accomplish miracles for him because some miracle such as that is needed if his political friends are going to achieve the results they want.
That, Mr. Chairman, is the second phase of this matter to which I want to draw his attention, the conservation and control of our own territorial waters. I am not going to develop it further at the moment but I hope that before the item passes the minister will clarify the position of his department and the government with respect to this matter.

Mr. Chairman, I should like first of all to thank members wishing to speak on the first item of the fisheries estimates who have given way to me because I will be away this afternoon and for the next few days. I should like to say that I am greatly pleased to see the Minister of Fisheries taking an active part in administering the affairs of his department. I followed very closely the serious injuries he received in Russia last year. I think most hon. members in this house realized that the minister possessed an abundance of mental and physical energy, much more than many of us in this house possess. I feel it is quite possible that this abundance of energy stood him in good stead. He has made a partial recovery at least and I hope that in the very near future recovery will be complete.
Since taking over the administration of the Department of Fisheries, the minister, I feel, has displayed a great interest in his department. We had evidence of this only last week when he invited members from the Atlantic provinces to meet with him and exchange views on the administration of his department. He afforded Liberal members from the four Atlantic provinces an opportunity of expressing their views and making suggestions with regard to the administration of his department. This procedure is contrary to an editorial f read in Maclean's magazine, the issue of March 3. I quote what the editor said:
Anyone who has been glancing lately at Hansard or at a reasonably good newspaper must have been reminded that parliament has ceased to be the chief official critic of the nation's conduct and its conscience. Much worse, the parliament of Canada has ceased to be. in any real sense, the government of Canada. It still has the power to
Supply-Fisheries
govern. Nevertheless, it continues to acquiesce blindly in all cabinet actions and pronouncements- voting almost as dependably on its party lines as that final horror of legislative horrors, the Supreme Soviet of the U.S.S.R.
In reply to that accusation which is directly applied to all Liberal backbench members, I want to say that only recently the Minister of National Health and Welfare invited members to a study group meeting on the administration of his department. I can recall numerous instances in the past when the Minister of Trade and Commerce has also welcomed members of the Liberal party to discuss the affairs of his department. It is stated very often in the press and in this house that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is, in reality, a dictator. In my opinion his treatment of the backbench members in inviting them to discuss matters of policy in connection with his department does not savour of dictatorship.
Leaving that matter now, because I do not wish to take up too much of the time of the house, I shall refer to some of the problems of the fishing industry in our province. The fishing industry in our province has been making great strides in the past few years with the assistance and co-operation of the federal and provincial governments. In the speech from the throne at the opening of the provincial legislature, the premier of our province, Mr. A. W. Matheson, announced he will establish a department of fisheries. He is to be commended for this action. Prior to this time fishing interests were taken care of by the department of industry and natural resources. I am sure that the fishermen of our province will greatly appreciate the move to set up the department of fisheries because I think it recognizes the position of the fisherman in our economic life and that has been long overdue.
I was interested in a remark the minister made when he said that, after discussion with his officials, it might be possible to establish a floor price for dogfish. He mentioned the west coast particularly, but if such a policy can be adopted by his department I should like to see it applied to the east coast also. In the months of July and August our fisheries are very seriously handicapped by an invasion of these fish. If the livers were worth something and something could be realized from the fish through processing them into fish meal, it might be that it would not cost the Department of Fisheries a great deal to provide an inducement to fish those predators. I am sure that our fishermen, who normally fish for hake, cod, and haddock after the close of the lobster fishing season, which is June 1 in our area, would be very pleased to fish for these dogfish.

Supply-Fisheries
I should like to say a word about a problem that has confronted me particularly. It relates to a branch of the shellfish industry in our province, namely quahaugs. There are large quantities of quahaugs present in polluted waters in our province. I understand that as a result of some arrangement between the public health department in the United States and the same department in Canada, there is a prohibition against taking fish from polluted waters, and that is quite reasonable. But in the case of some mollusks, such as oysters, permission is granted to transplant them to other areas for recleansing purposes. I took the matter up with the two departments last year. Both departments are involved in this question, but evidently the stumbling block was that no scientific research had been carried on up to this time as to how long a quahaug should be placed on a beach to be purified.
The minister and his officials in one meeting suggested it might be possible to recleanse the quahaugs in pounds. I like that suggestion very much. I believe it was made by Dr. Pritchard because of the fact that it would save the cost of reraking the fish from any beaches where they might have been relaid for recleansing purposes. However, I hope we can get permission to relay. I am most anxious that we eventually will, because on the return of a heavy volume of seaweed these hard-shell clams will eventually die. There is a market for them in Canada. They are ground into meat and sold in Canada. They are not sold in the United States because there is no market for them. I understand that in the United States they use only the tender small quahaugs called littlenecks. It would give us a lot of employment. It is estimated that the industry would be worth in the vicinity of $100,000 a year to the labour employed in the transplanting of the quahaugs from those areas to other areas for purification purposes and their repossession and processing.
I know the minister is most deeply interested in this, and I hope that he shall have permission in the very near future to transplant these quahaugs.
I also like the suggestion made by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), who preceded me in this debate, that it is most unfair for those who are financed and equipped with draggers by both the federal Department of Fisheries and the provincial department of fisheries to encroach on the inshore boats. They should at least keep off three miles. We have had that difficulty at home, and our dragger fishermen are now realizing why it is a great discouragement to the inshore fishing boats to

fish when their gear is being taken up by larger vessels. In that connection I should like to say that at Souris we have one fresh fish filleting plant and two by-products plants that have been in operation for two or three years. In the coming season we shall have another large fresh fish filleting plant operating at Souris. I hope that sufficient encouragement will be given to the inshore fishing boats to fish cod, hake, flounder and haddock after the close of the lobster fishing season at some fishing centres.
These inshore boats have been fishing in past years. I know of one case where fish have been trucked as far as 30 miles from where they are landed to the fresh fish filleting plant. I would like to see all the lobster inshore boats fish, as I have already mentioned, at the close of the lobster fishing season. I would also hope that the processing plants could pay sufficient money for their fish to induce those fishermen to go out and fish and have the fish brought to the processing fish centres. It would be a great advantage because dry periods are experienced by the dragging fishing vessels, and the inshore fishing boats would supplement the supply and would provide for continuous operation of the plant and continuous employment of the employees.
I have just another word, Mr. Chairman, before I close. I should like to say that because of the assistance that has been given by the federal government by way of a subsidy of $65, per registered ton for boats over 40 feet in length, and also the assistance that has been given by the provincial department, we shall have about 15 draggers owned and operated in our own province this year. I think that with the intake from the inshore boats we can keep both of these processing plants and both of the by-product plants in full operation.

Mr. Chairman, I believe there is just time before I ask you to call it one o'clock to join with the other hon. members who have taken part in this debate so far in saying how pleased we are that this morning the Minister of Fisheries was able to be back in his seat and in the form he was when he gave us an outline of the activities of his department.
Like the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, I would have been very much interested if the minister had been able to give us a more extensive picture of some of his observations on fisheries while he was abroad. I realize that perhaps the estimates of his department may not be the most appropriate place for that to be done; but I do hope that the minister will keep that in mind and some time before the session is over will find

suitable opportunity to give to the house a picture of some of the things that he saw.
Would you call it one o'clock, Mr. Chairman?
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, at one o'clock I was about to enter into some comment concerning the first item of the fisheries estimates and some of the matters that appear to me to be of interest and concern at this time.
I think the minister made it clear this morning in his opening remarks, and probably it will appear even more clear in the statistics which he put on the record, that fisheries is now one of our great national industries and that it is wise for hon. members of this house to realize that what has become rather a trite saying, "There are only two great sources of food for the people of the world, the agricultural industry and the fisheries industry" is indeed true and that we in this country are blessed with a very rich heritage in both those fields of food resources.
Like the Minister of Fisheries, I come from a west coast constituency. I do not intend to attempt to enter into any extended discussion of the fisheries of the Atlantic coast or of our inland fisheries except to say that as a member of this house who has some appreciation of the value of this resource I am interested in the well-being of the great Atlantic fisheries. I am also interested in the fact that much remains to be done in that area before the economic value per pound of fish caught approaches that of the west coast. Those who live on the west coast realize that even with the present relationship in the markets of the world of the value of our product to the pound caught, our fishermen by and large do not enjoy anything more than a reasonable return for their efforts.
There is one aspect of the current fishery situation which appears to me to be of equal concern to the fishermen of the Atlantic coast and of the Pacific coast. Reference was made to this by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings when he was speaking of the matter of territorial waters. I would have been glad if the minister had been able to give us a positive assurance that this particular problem was on the way towards some satisfactory solution.
Supply-Fisheries
I was quite interested to read recently in the publication of the fisheries council of Canada a report on the present situation as it exists. This is one which I feel should be brought fully to the attention of the house. This report is an excerpt taken by them from the Financial Times published in Great Britain and it makes some reference to the international law commission and to the report which it has made. The gist of this report seems to me to be that we are entering into a veritable no-man's land of international law at the present time when we discuss the situation. It makes reference to the fact that various nations have been making a variety of claims in this connection. While I generally agree that we Canadians should attempt every means of reaching an amicable international understanding upon this question, I cannot help but wonder after having read this report whether or not the time has come for us to put forward, perhaps just a little more firmly than we may have done or than on the surface we appear to have done, our own feelings and our own position in relation to this situation.
I know that the minister is aware there is a strong feeling among the fishermen in British Columbia that we should assert our rights to territorial waters lying inside our offshore islands, Vancouver island and the Queen Charlotte islands. Certainly there are indications from the position taken in some instances by our neighbour the United States that we would not perhaps be doing anything in that respect that they have not done if we were to take that position. However, I do hope that it will not be long before the international law commission's report will produce some definite international action and international agreement on it.
There is one statement which I think points up the fact that this has come into the realm where people such as hon. members of parliament should be concerned about it. Referring to the opinion of the international law commission the bulletin of the fisheries council of Canada states on page 5:
It feels that the task of harmonizing the different views, which often originate in different political or economic conditions, should rather be entrusted to a diplomatic conference.
That, I take it, means that we in this parliament should be attempting to assist our government to crystallize its point of view on this'subject. As far as I can see, and I am expressing only my own opinion on this matter, there should be little question that Canada should be willing to stand for a recognition of territorial waters, at least as far as fishing is concerned, to the 12-mile limit and that we should be behind the idea

Supply-Fisheries
of developing international recognition for the inclusion of waters which lie inside our headlands in addition to that 12-mile limit.
I admit, Mr. Speaker, that since I have been coming to Ottawa I have had an opportunity of acquiring more knowledge of some of the eastern species of fish. I will even go so far as to confess that I have developed an appreciation of some of the products such as the haddock and the cod that come from the Atlantic coast. I would suggest to those who come from the Atlantic provinces that if they would only be willing to overcome the foolish idea which they try to promulgate, that there is some basis for favourable comparison between what they call salmon and what we produce in British Columbia, those of us from the Pacific coast would probably be willing to participate in an all-out sort of co-operation in developing a wider appreciation of all the fishing products that are produced.
In this connection I may say that as a result of visits that were made to the test kitchen of the Department of Fisheries my wife has been trying out on me some of the recipes that come from there and the results by and large have been quite favourable. That may have something to do with increasing my appreciation of eastern fisheries products.
By and large.

An hon. member says, "By and large". I do not believe in being too unqualified in public praise. While I am on this subject of the different fisheries I must confess that I have been shocked in recent weeks to discover from conversations with hon. members in this house that many do not realize that we have a herring fishery on the west coast. For that reason I think I should draw attention to the fact that the minister's statistics will reveal that the west coast herring fishery is larger than the Atlantic coast herring fishery and from the point of view of total tonnage caught represents something more than half the total poundage of fish products produced in British Columbia.
There was one problem which the minister did not deal with this morning and on which I had hoped he would make a statement. Perhaps he will find an opportunity before these estimates pass to do so. I refer to the widespread concern over the mid-Pacific salmon fishing. Many fishermen of British Columbia are firmly convinced that the -salmon being taken in the mid-Pacific are immature and should properly be caught after reaching maturity by our fishermen closer to shore. They feel that something should be done in the way of immediate action to prevent the taking of these salmon, principally by Japanese vessels. I do not think the

minister will feel that it is necessary for me to expand upon the rather unfortunate implications that might arise out of a growth of this feeling in British Columbia.
