I think it would be worth while if we had some explanation of what is being done in this connection and also some factual information as to what the situation is from the scientific point of view in regard to the claim that we are losing a large potential salmon fishery as a result of the mid-Pacific fishing.
I was glad the minister made some reference to the problem created by the increasing depredations of dogfish. This is a particular problem facing the fishermen who fish in the waters between Vancouver island and the mainland. They are increasingly concerned over the destruction of nets and gear and the increasing effects of dogfish upon the salmon fishery. I hope that this problem will be resolved in a way which will make it possible for the fishermen to utilize to advantage some of their time during the off season for other species.
It is true, as the minister pointed out, that there was a drop in the income from our fisheries last year and this has resulted in the fishermen of British Columbia taking an increased interest in the question which was discussed last year of providing access to the benefits of the Unemployment Insurance Act. I know that this matter as it affects the fishermen of the Atlantic coast has been drawn to the attention of the committee already and I recognize also that it is not a matter coming directly under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Fisheries, but nevertheless I think it would be appropriate at this time if I were to urge him to use his influence toward a solution of this problem- perhaps I should say to continue to use his influence, because he did give us some assurances along this line last year in the industrial relations committee.
There is another matter which I feel is of some concern and which is brought to my mind by the salmon spawning report issued by the able chief supervisor of fisheries in British Columbia for 1955. I raise this matter because, to me at least, it involves a question of policy extending beyond the activities of the Department of Fisheries. In the annual report of the department which we have just received reference is made to some of the activities of the protection and fish culture branches. In respect to the salmon spawning streams it is pointed out that the fishery officers of the protection branch have continued their program of fry salvage and stream clearance throughout the year. It is stated that over one hundred streams had

log jams, rocks and debris removed. That reference will be found on pages 17 and 18 of the report.
I do not quarrel with the fact that that activity has been and will be of continuing value, but I think the report of the chief supervisor of fisheries on spawning makes it clear that that program of itself is not enough. Running through his analyses of spawning of various salmon species over the past year like a refrain is reference to the fact that in many instances what might have been a satisfactory spawning situation was ruined because of flood damage. In one report, referring to the spawning of chum salmon, it states:
Here again flood damage resulting from the storm of November 2nd and 3rd caused extensive damage to the early spawning. Some damage also resulted to the moderately good supplies in the Squamish system.
Then referring to the Victoria area it has this to say:
It is estimated, however, that 75 per cent of the spawn deposition in these streams was destroyed by the November flash flood.
I bring this matter to the attention of the committee because I think it involves policies beyond those which the Department of Fisheries can exercise.
If the Department of Fisheries, which is charged with the responsibility of protecting and increasing our salmon runs, is going to be able to do the job that it should be doing there must come about a recognition that part and parcel of the policy which will make this increase in our valuable salmon industry possible is in the development of a program of stream control. Perhaps this is a subject that might very well have come up during the recent discussion on conservation introduced by the hon. member for Kootenay West. In fact, had it not been that there seemed to be a great number of speakers interested in that debate, I might very well have had something to say about it then.
To me this is obviously a problem that is going to require co-operation between federal and provincial authorities. It is going to require a plan which involves our forest industry and involves almost every aspect of soil and water conservation. I bring it up now to urge that consideration of this problem beyond that merely of the Department of Fisheries be given by the government. It seems to me that the activity that is being carried on in a modest way in respect to clearing log jams, out of streams, and so on, is going to have little value unless a much broader program is developed that will result in measures being taken to eliminate the flash flooding, which, as the chief supervisor
Supply-Fisheries
has pointed out, has almost destroyed satisfactory spawning in many of the areas during the past year.
There are quite a number of other items that I have noted. I should like to bring up some of them when we are discussing the details of the estimates. But there are a few more problems here on which I should appreciate a clearcut statement from the minister.
One of the questions that has been asked of me is as to the eligibility of the Indian fishermen of British Columbia to qualify for loans under the act that was passed last year. I should hope that the minister could give a clearcut statement on that point so that there could be no misunderstanding of the actual situation.
Another question that is of concern to some of the Indian fishermen who live in the vicinity of Ripple Rock is as to what the effect upon their fishery is going to be when that big blast is set off. Some of them are fearful that not only will there be some destruction of the migratory stocks of fish that are in that area at the time but that the result of the blast will be such as to entirely wipe out the local stocks of ground fish and will leave them without access to winter subsistence Ashing, on which they rely for part of their food. I would appreciate having some statement based on the best available evidence as to what the results of that blast will be in that respect.
I think that covers all the points that I shall attempt to deal with at this time. There are one or two other matters, but I note that the time at my disposal now will not allow me to enter into discussion of them and so I shall defer them for consideration at a later time.

I am sure it has been an inspiration to all members who have listened to the introductory remarks of the Minister of Fisheries today as he outlined the work of his department. I remember that on other occasions when he has made the opening speech in connection with his estimates we always felt that he gave a very vivid outline of all the activities that come under his jurisdiction. He has the happy knack of not only giving information but imparting some inspiration with it as well, and certainly his remarks today have been no exception to that rule.
I should like to join with the other members who have extended a welcome back to the Minister of Fisheries. We followed with concern the reports of his accident and illness and we were in hopes that the time would not be too long before he would be back here to

Supply-Fisheries
assume his responsibilities in the department and in the house. So 1 join with the others who welcome him back and wish him continued health. I should be very much interested to hear of his impressions and his observations on his recent trip to Asia. I am sure he gleaned a great deal of valuable information and, when the opportune time presents itself and he does speak on that matter, I am sure it will be of real interest to all members of the house.
I should like to say that I regret that the hon. member for New Westminster is not here today to take part in this debate. He was called away because of death in his family; otherwise he would have been participating on this first occasion in this debate. I am sure his analysis of the situation and his outline of the problems would have been much more detailed than I shall be able to give today, but he may be back in time to participate before the conclusion of the debate.
We have been reminded of the continued and increasing importance of the fishing industry to the economy of Canada. We have learned a great deal since the opening of the session on the importance of the agricultural industry, and we who come from non-wheatgrowing areas listened with real interest to those debates. Now we hope that the members from the prairie provinces will bear with us as we discuss some of the problems relevant to the industry that is very vital to us, namely, the fishing industry.
Last fall there was a great deal of concern over the fact that first reports were to the effect that the salmon industry was going to suffer some severe setbacks, but we were encouraged again to read further reports that what had been lost through the depletion of the catch of the sockeye was being made up to quite an extent by the catch of pinks. I shall just refer to a brief article in the Vancouver Daily Province of September 22, 1955:
Big Run on Pinks Aids Salmon Trade.
A huge run of pink salmon at the last moment has saved the British Columbia fishing industry from one of the worst years on record.
Eventual catch of pinks by the end of the season is expected to nearly equal the record catch of one million cases set more than 25 years ago.
A. J. Whitmore, chief fisheries supervisor, said the result has been that this has become "a good average year".
I met some of the fishermen at about the time when their prospects were rather dark. They were very much concerned over the situation and wondered how they were going to be able to carry on operations and finance their domestic programs through the coming year. Another matter of real concern is the damage caused by floods to which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has referred. This was emphasized in one of the local papers 
in my own area, the Fraser Valley Record of November of last year. In that paper it is stated:
A preliminary review of potential damage caused by the recent storm and record rainfall in the lower mainland areas shows that many important salmon spawning areas suffered severe losses. Most seriously affected was the recent pink salmon spawning in lower Fraser streams; in several instances the results almost suggest a state of disaster and where the local fisheries officers feel that 10 per cent survival of a large spawning is the best that might be hoped for.
In connection with the spawning areas, I should like to refer to a brief article that was handed to me. It is taken from the New York Times of February 28, 1956. It is rather strange that the information as to this particular project should come to me from New York, but no doubt it is because of my inability to keep up with all the reading material that we receive from the different departments. The article is entitled, "Salmon Eggs Aided by Canadian Science". It is a Canadian Press report from Nanaimo, British Columbia, and reads:
Reduction of the losses of salmon eggs on British Columbia spawning beds is the aim of scientists at the Pacific biological station near here. Field tests on a strip of the Fraser river resulted in reducing mortality rate to 35 per cent from an average of 90 per cent, one scientist reported. Ability of water to flow through gravel and provide oxygen to eggs while removing noxious substances from egg clusters is under close study. The findings are expected to disclose the type of gravel best suited to spawning beds and may lead to creation of artificial spawning beds in streams, the scientist said.
This brief article concludes:
One expert said the day may come when bulldozers will prepare spawning beds with specified gravel on a gradient sufficient to provide a predetermined flow of water through the gravel.
When the minister concludes the debate on this item perhaps he might refer to that matter and enlarge upon it for our benefit.
We were very happy to hear the minister state today that domestic consumption of fishery products is rising. I remember participating in the debate on another occasion when I referred to the assistance that might be given in the matter of training chefs. I do not know whether or not that has anything to do with the situation. Culinary techniques may be improving, but we are glad that there is an increase in the domestic consumption of fish and this no doubt will reflect itself in the industry.
We are also glad that there are no surpluses on hand. I believe this is very encouraging for the fishing industry. The minister referred to the various international commissions that had been set up and made particular mention of two of them. One of them was the commission set up under the great lakes convention. We were interested

to learn that the Canadian government has already taken action to set the machinery in motion in this respect, and we wish the commission every success as it tackles the problem of the lamprey eels about which we heard so much last session. We hope that its efforts will result in the rehabilitation of the fisheries on the great lakes.
At that time we were privileged to see some films provided under the auspices of the fisheries department. One of them had to do with the lamprey eel, and there was also one on the lobster fishery. I was wondering whether it would not be possible this session to have further films shown with respect to our fisheries and fishery activities. I am sure they would be of tremendous interest and of great benefit to us in getting a better picture of the entire fishing industry. If it is possible we would certainly be happy to see that done.
Reference was also made to the international Pacific salmon commission and to the stringent regulations that have been recommended by way of a conservation program. Whatever steps may be necessary to conserve this vital industry will, I am sure, receive the co-operation of the industry when such steps have definitely been proven to be necessary and their efficiency has been established.
There is one matter to which reference was not made and which was not mentioned by the minister. I have not heard anything recently respecting the efforts to secure an international treaty on pinks. It may be that something has been done in this connection but I have not had any report brought to my attention, or if I have I have forgotten it. Perhaps the minister might refer to that matter and bring us up to date on the efforts that have been made and the negotiations that have been instituted. I believe I remember that last year the minister referred to the fact that now that there has been more or less of an equalization of the catch between the Canadian and United States fisheries the United States might be more willing to agree to such a convention.
I should like to refer to the fisheries on the Fraser river. Our fishermen have had their difficulties in the past, and on different occasions we have had the opportunity of bringing various problems to the attention of the minister and the house. Some of them still continue. An announcement was made to the effect that earlier closures were to be instituted on the Fraser river as a conservation measure and also to safeguard the quality of fish being caught. I understand that this year closure is to go into effect on the 15th of September.
Supply-Fisheries
There are two questions I should like to ask the minister in this connection which he might answer a little later in the debate. First of all, I should like to know if the minister is absolutely convinced that the results obtained have justified the action taken with respect to earlier closure on the Fraser above the New Westminster bridge. Second, is the minister contemplating any further changes in these regulations, either by way of modification or to make them even more stringent than at present? In this connection I might say that some of the fishermen are under the impression that this is the last year that fishing in that area is to be permitted. I hope the minister will clarify this matter and also let us know whether any other regulations are being considered in this regard.
Of real concern, of course, to those in the Fraser valley and in other sections as well is the discussion that is at present going on with respect to fishing and power, and to which the minister referred in his address. We all know somewhat of the proposed development of the power potential of the Fraser river. I think all concerned are in agreement on the necessity of protecting the valuable fisheries industry. The minister referred to the harmonious relations existing between all concerned in this matter, the fisheries department, the provincial government and the power industry.
I have the report of the fisheries association of British Columbia the "Facts on Fish",
dated January 24, 1956. The first two paragraphs are as follows:
Recognition that the Fraser river is primarily a salmon stream and should be protected as such was the gratifying conclusion to be drawn from the recent announcement of the formation oi Western Development and Power, Limited, a subsidiary of the British Columbia Power Corporation.
The announcement by Dal Grauer, President of British Columbia Power Corporation, declared the two principal functions of the newly formed company would be
"(1) To develop hydroelectric power on the Fraser river to the extent that the maintenance of salmon spawning will allow and on the Columbia river where there is no salmon problem, and (2) To study industrial opportunities in the areas which can be served with this power and to bring in new industries to use it."
The fishing industry commends Mr. Grauer and his company for their aims and ambitions.
The fourth paragraph in this report is as follows:
In a public statement following the announcement, Mr. E. L. Harrison, Vice Chairman of the fisheries association declared the B.C. Power Corporation's announcement was of the greatest significance to the future welfare of British Columbia. It put into sharp focus the principle that preservation of the salmon resource for the benefit of all

Supply-Fisheries
Canadians is of top priority in the planning for the future by governments and most interested industries, he said.
Then this report refers also to the gift that has been made to the University of British Columbia by the power corporation for research work in this connection. I am reminded, too, of the statement made by the minister that Mr. H. R. MacMillan has made a contribution of $100,000 to the same research program. The Vancouver board of trade, as revealed in this same report from the fisheries association of British Columbia, lends its support to the attitude taken by the various authorities.
On page 2 of the report we find this:
A resolution which reflects the sentiments of the influential Vancouver board of trade was submitted to the provincial government last month and its contents was of great importance to the fishing industry. Following a preamble which pointed up the need for preservation of the fishing industry the resolution stated:
I am just going to read the first three items because they refer specifically to the matter under discussion.
1.	The board endorses the policy of the provincial government which is to expand the industrial output of this province, to develop the interior and northern areas and to wisely use and conserve our natural resources for the overall benefit of the people of British Columbia.
2.	The board endorses the policy of the provincial government that no hydro developments will be permitted on commercial salmon producing rivers until it is proven that such developments will not adversely affect the salmon fisheries in any serious degree.
3.	The board believes that the present and potential water of "non-fish" rivers should be utilized for the development of hydro-power before applications are considered for the use of water for such purpose on fish streams in order that increased hydro-power may be available while scientific work continues on the still unsolved problem of up and down stream migration of salmon past dams.
The view of the provincial government, as referred to by the Minister of Fisheries, was that no licence should be issued until this problem is overcome.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer. I am just going to refer to it, and I am not going to spend any time enlarging upon it. I should like to mention the suggested diversion of the flood waters of the Columbia river into the Fraser. No doubt we have read the statement made by the chairman of the international Pacific salmon fisheries commission in this connection. Apparently he is very hesitant about placing any approval whatever on such a program. He refers to the different problems which must be overcome such as water temperature, content of water and so on, all of which could be seriously affected by the diversion
(Mr. Patterson.]
of glacial waters into the Fraser river. I want to refer to an article in the Vancouver Province of Thursday, December 8, 1955, written by Alan Jessup. In this article we have a reference to this proposal, and I quote: Furthermore, the suggestion of increasing the Fraser's power potential by diverting the head waters of the Columbia into the Fraser, also makes salmon interests shudder.
Fishermen argue that changes in water temperatures in spawning rivers have a direct effect on the survival of fingerlings. They contend that to divert waters on one river into another with subsequent changes in temperature could cause untold damage. It is further suggested that the Columbia, fed from ice fields, may be colder than the Fraser.
Fortunately fishing and power interests have graduated from the initial intolerance each displayed toward the other. Both are anxious to reach a compromise. But on the cold, hard facts of the salmon's life cycle there is not too much room for compromise.
I am sure every safeguard will be taken and this matter will be thoroughly investigated before any action is taken.
I should like to make just a brief reference to the matter of fishermen and their relation to unemployment insurance benefits. I have a letter from the United Fishermen and Allied Workers' Union dated August 11, 1955. I should like to quote one paragraph which has a special reference to this matter.
As you are no doubt aware, our union has been campaigning for a number of years for unemploy ment insurance to be provided to all commercial fishermen. We were very disturbed to find that parliament did not move more forcibly in the direction of unemployment insurance for fishermen at the last session.
We noted there were promises made to the effect that there would be further investigation and hope expressed in the near future commercial fishermen would obtain coverage under the Unemployment Insurance Act. However, these promises and hopes will not answer the critical problems facing the commercial fishermen of British Columbia this year. That is why we are writing to you at this time and urging you to take immediate action on behalf of the fishermen.
I had the privilege of attending a very large meeting of the fishermen last fall in the city of New Westminster where this was one of the matters under discussion and consideration. At that meeting we were requested to give our support to their proposals and their request for unemployment insurance benefits. In this connection, it was suggested that in order to assure the coverage of fishermen by this act coverage should be extended to all bona fide commercial fishermen whether they were gill netters, seiners or trawlers, and also for the purposes of the act the buyer of the catch should be classified as an employer.
I believe it is one of the problems that was mentioned, to designate the employer relationship.
At that meeting a certain survey that was conducted by the unemployment insurance

commission in 1951 was referred to. I have not seen the report, but it was referred to in that meeting. In that survey it was stated that the problem of establishing employer relationship would not be insuperable. It also suggested that the obvious person would be the purchaser of the catch. I just pass these suggestions along from this meeting of the fishermen which I had the privilege to attend. I am sure that in the consideration of this matter the unions would have other suggestions which would be of assistance. I hope the minister will make some reference to this matter when he closes the debate.
These are some of the matters that I wanted to bring to the attention of the minister at this time. I repeat, we are vitally interested in this industry; we know the Minister of Fisheries is also vitally interested in it. His enthusiasm and energy are appreciated, and I trust that in the further continued administration of his department every possible way will be explored to extend the value of this industry in the economy of Canada.

Mr. Chairman, before coming to the remarks which I wish to make on this item I should like to associate myself with the sentiments that have been expressed by previous speakers and say how glad I am to see the minister back in his seat again and restored once more to his usual health and vigour. I should like also to compliment him on the clear and concise exposition which he gave us this morning on the introduction of his estimates, and also on his vivid and graphic description of the problem facing his department, particularly on the west coast.
May I also say how pleasant it is to hear the word "fish" once more after sitting continuously for days on end and hearing nothing but wheat, wheat, wheat for the past three weeks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Order.

In his remarks this morning the minister indicated that the over-all general picture was a little better than that of last year. This, of course, is not true in my own riding, and I do not think it is true in the over-all picture of my own province. The production was spotty, particularly in the shore fishery, and our production of light salted cod, our traditional product, was about 200,000 quintals lower than the previous year.
The minister expressed gratification at the continued expansion of fresh fish production. Continued expansion, of course, is good only if markets are available to absorb the surplus catch. There is a very great danger of over-production which would result of course in a softening of prices and lower returns to the fishermen.
Supply-Fisheries
As far as Newfoundland is concerned, continued expansion of fresh fish production at the expense of salt fish production would be little short of a calamity. In my opinion we have already proceeded too far along this road. The fresh fish industry alone cannot bring maximum prosperity to our Newfoundland fishermen for the simple reason that when the fish are running the fresh fish processing plants cannot handle the amount of fish that the fishermen can catch, and consequently their production is limited to the capacity of the plant.
In Newfoundland, expansion of the fresh and salt fish industry should go hand-in-hand so that the surplus fish which the plants are unable to handle could be put up in salted or pickled form. Our two greatest needs in Newfoundland are expansion of markets and outlets and a greater diversification of our fisheries and fish products so that the fisherman can be employed continuously at his occupation and at the same time be able to sell all the fish that he can produce.
Personally, I am a great believer in the future of the salt fish industry. In spite of the difficulties now being experienced, I believe that from the long-range point of view it can become more stable and less vulnerable than the fresh fish industry. There will always be a market for salt fish because it is an essential food and a valuable source of protein and salt which are essential to the health and nourishment of peoples who live in hot climates.
I believe the time will come when our own traditional markets, our traditional Mediterranean markets, will expand once more to their former proportions. In the very nature of things, as a result of industrial forces such as automation, as well as of other forces, sociological and ideological, the time must come when the people of Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece will enjoy a much higher standard of living than they do today. That day may be long delayed, but it is certain to come, and when it arrives our fish will then be more competitive in those markets. I also look forward to the day when we shall once more be sending salt fish to Brazil, which at one time took as many as half a million quintals from us. Brazil is a country blessed with tremendous national wealth and the day will come when that wealth will be developed and Brazil will be on her way to economic recovery. Anything that we as a nation can do to hasten that day \trill be of great benefit to Newfoundland because Brazil can absorb practically our total production of salt fish.
The recovery of the salt cod industry is, of course, dependent upon quality production. I had hoped that the minister would have made some reference to bonus payments for

Supply-Fisheries
choice and prime Italian and Spanish cures to encourage quality production for those markets.
The minister referred this morning to the salt rebate which he announced last year. On the whole I believe that the salt rebate has been fairly successful although of course in the minds of fishermen it has not been anything like the cash equivalent of the price support payments or deficiency payments which they had formerly received. There is, however, one aspect of this salt rebate question which is worthy of consideration. Because the amount of salt used in producing heavy salted fish is almost twice as much as that which is used in producing light salted fish, one effect of the rebate has been to encourage the production of heavy salted fish at the expense of the production of light salted fish. It is estimated that possibly we could have sold 200,000 quintals more of light salted fish than what was produced. Light salted fish is, after all, our traditional product. History tells us that the light salted fish in Newfoundland goes back to the days of the Napoleonic wars when the British fleet had blockaded the coast of eastern Europe and supplies of salt were not available. Necessity became the mother of invention and our people developed the process of curing the fish with about half the amount of salt they would normally use. This came to be a very distinctive product of Newfoundland, one that was specially favoured in Mediterranean markets and one that we must endeavour to keep at all costs.
If we are to encourage the production of light salted fish and offset the effect of the present salt rebate we should have a different rate of rebate for light salted fish from that which we have for heavy salted fish. In fact, to equalize the two, the rebate should be doubled or practically 100 per cent on light salted fish. It certainly should not be less than 90 per cent. This would also benefit the fishermen of Nova Scotia because it would prevent an oversupply of heavy salted fish which would tend to soften the prices in the Nova Scotian markets.
While I am speaking about the salt rebate, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out to the minister that the forms drawn up in connection with this rebate are far too complicated for the ordinary fisherman to cope with; indeed, one would almost require a college degree to be able to fill them out correctly. Some of the fishermen in my own constituency had great difficulty with these forms and they were very resentful of the fact that after having received assistance from the teacher, the priest, or the magistrate or whoever came along, these forms were returned

for correction after considerable delay and in some cases the amount of salt that they used was questioned.
In transactions involving the purchase and selling of salt fish there is a great need for much more uniformity in weights and measures than exists at the present time. For example, in Newfoundland 1 hundredweight of fish is 112 pounds. In the maritimes 1 hundredweight of fish is 100 pounds. The Newfoundland fisherman who sells his fish by the hundredweight therefore has a loss of about 12 per cent on his transaction as compared with his counterpart on the mainland. To solve this problem I would suggest that regulations should be drawn up which would compel that fish be sold everywhere by the pound.
There is also a wide discrepancy in the way fish are measured which has a very distinct bearing on the cull. In Newfoundland the length of a fish is measured as the distance between the hollow part of the nape and the small part of the tail. On the mainland the length of the fish is the total over-all length from the peak of the nape to the tip of the tail. Thus an 8-inch fish which would be classed as a small fish in Newfoundland would be considered well over a 12-inch fish on the mainland. Similarly an 18-inch fish which would be considered as medium in Newfoundland would be classed as being over 22 inches in the maritimes, which results in a much greater return due to the difference in cull.
I should also like to see established the practice of selling and using salt by weight instead of by volume. In this way I believe we could develop a much more definite and precise line of distinction between fish classed as heavy salted and that which is called light salted. At the present time, with salt being used by the volume, there is a great deal of overlapping and different degrees of heavy and light salted fish, which is not in the best interests of quality production.
I said a few minutes ago that our greatest needs are more outlets and greater diversification. More imagination is needed in the development of fish products. In addition to the different ways in which salted and pickled fish can be processed I believe more attention should be given to the canning of fish, both fresh and salted. For example, fish cakes can be made either from fresh or salted fish and in each case they are delicious when served with onions and potatoes. I believe a product could be made up which would prove most acceptable in the domestic market. I hope that in time it may be possible to develop a food product made up of a blend of fish proteins and wheat, something which is causing so much trouble for our friends

on the prairies. We would thus be able to kill two birds with one stone.
I was glad to hear the minister refer this morning to the extension of the domestic market and in this connection I should like to pay a tribute to the Canadian National . Railways for the lead they have given in the development of the Canex container. Now anyone who travels on the Canadian National Railways can enjoy a meal of delicious fish made possible by the use of this container. I hope that samples of this fish will be made available in our parliamentary restaurant and perhaps the minister could arrange with Mr. Donald Gordon to have samples cooked up in the Union station restaurant and at other stations along the railroad. He might consider also giving out samples to advertise this quality product.
Since the Newfoundland minister is the minister of immigration perhaps samples of Italian cured fish could be made up and presented to Italian immigrants when they come to this country. On second thought, perhaps it would be worth while to ship samples overseas to be distributed to prospective applicants before they even consider coming to this country.
I have said before that our two chief needs are markets and outlets and diversification. I give those two prior position over the means of production because I think it is unbusinesslike to consider improving the means of production until we have found a way to dispose of all we can catch with the means of production we now have.
However, there is considerable interest in the mechanization of our fisheries in Newfoundland and in this connection I should like to point out to the minister the need of a more flexible system of bounties than we now have. Many of my fishermen are not taking advantage of the federal bounty because in order to do so they must build a boat which they consider is far heavier than they need. Being far heavier it would be more expensive to handle, to keep up and maintain, and when the planks became waterlogged after a few years she would be heavier in the water and therefore more difficult to propel. I would suggest that the present system of bounties be revised so that they would be available for much smaller boats than is now the case. I think perhaps there could be two or three classes, perhaps for boats of ten tons and boats of twenty tons.
I should like to say something about the bait service but I shall deal with this matter at greater length when that particular item is before the committee.
Supply-Fisheries
I was disappointed this morning when the minister made no reference to unemployment insurance benefits for fishermen. When the prices support item is before the committee I hope to say a few words on that subject and discuss the problem of stabilizing the fisherman's income.
Before I close I should like to say a word about the fisheries development program. I believe that what we need is an over-all program which would embrace, not only Newfoundland but all the Atlantic provinces. I think we are making a big mistake in going about our fisheries development program piecemeal without any correlation or integration. We have plenty of competitors in the world markets without having to spend time and energy competing among ourselves. I believe that if we take this approach to the problem it will be much better in the long run, not only for the fishermen of my province but for all the fishermen of eastern Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to refer briefly and generally to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects and the treatment that it gave to the fisheries field generally. Someone has said that if the Gordon commission did nothing else but get Canadians to imagine what their country will be 20 or 30 years from now it will have justified its existence.
Fisheries were referred to in the excellent brief presented by the fisheries council of Canada, and I understand also that some of the provinces dealt with fisheries in their own briefs. I have not had time to read and study the fisheries council brief in detail, but I should like to refer briefly to four or five points which were mentioned as being of importance. Significantly they are points that have future consideration which I think is most important in the fisheries business today.
The first reference was to immigration. I think it would be an excellent idea to consider the immigration of fishermen to Canada. This could be handled somewhat like the agricultural worker. These men could be induced to come here with their special training and thus add something to our culture. There would be limitations upon what could be done with them. I suppose it would be necessary to insist that they stay in their intended occupation and perhaps some assistance could be given. It is an excellent idea and I do not anticipate that there would be much difficulty with the present minister of immigration, who appreciates the sea and fishermen and all that is connected with them. The minister of immigration has a further interest in the sea now that he is the owner of a small vessel.

Supply-Fisheries
In their brief the fisheries council dealt also with power plants constructed on our streams and rivers, and their effects upon the fishing industry. The Minister of Fisheries has gone in considerable detail into the problems out west. We have exactly the same problem on the Saint John river. I shall not mention that, but there is a further problem that is of a slightly different nature. That concerns the power dams that are being discussed now with regard to the bay of Fundy itself. Of course, as has been mentioned in the past, the future of the fishing industry will have to be seriously considered if this dam takes shape in the bay of Fundy.
I was interested to hear the minister mention that out west experiments have been made in training the fish to follow various scents at dams. I do not remember whether the minister said they followed noise or sounds, but I read in the newspaper a short while ago that at Bowdoin college in Maine they have been able to train fish or cause them to follow various musical notes, and they expect that in the future a pied piper going up and down the banks of the river will lead the fish through the various obstacles that may be there.
Third, mention was made in their brief, and rightly so, of federal aid for research. Last night I managed to squeeze in a few remarks regarding fisheries research in the discussion on the research committee. Most of the members took the opportunity to get into the atomic field, but I feel-and I know the minister agrees-that it is very important that federal aid and federal research generally be discussed and stimulated through this new field that is open to us now.
In regard to the Saltonstall-Kennedy hearings in the United States which I mentioned last night, with which I know the minister is quite fapailiar, it was not the legislation, perhaps, that was important; it was the fact that so many experts attended and so much publicity was given to the hearings when the committee was considering this bill in 1954. I feel that would tie in with future needs, the stimulation and interest that would be given in our research committee if fisheries were on the list of subjects.
I do not wish to say any more on that except to repeat what I said last night, that I realize the minister is research-conscious.
I also know that the fisheries department has a very commendable research program now. It has about a half or three quarters of the landed catch invested in research but, after all, we do need more money and better research. The investment will be returned in the future.

Fourth, the United States markets were mentioned. I was quite pleased to see the fisheries research council mention this, because we are very much concerned about those markets. I do not want to go into a discussion of tariffs in general here, but I feel that in the maritimes now we have something good in the fish sticks, something the United States market wants. We feel it is a hardship to be taxed so heavily by tariffs that it is almost impossible to get finished sticks into the United States market. We are always going to have an unfavourable balance of trade with the United States, as things look now. Why not take cognizance of that fact and compensate for it by recognizing that we have a product here that the people in the United States want? It could not possibly disrupt any other markets. We want to ' encourage this industry, and it would help us to be able to export one of the few finished products we shall ever have.
Those are the remarks the fisheries council made. May I just refer briefly to the New Brunswick brief presented to the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, which dealt briefly with the fishing industry in that province. Some early history was mentioned at the beginning of their brief, and they brought the picture up to the post-war period when they were, quite rightly, hopeful of the future. The capital investment and the general catch has been good since 1945, and they made note of that.
The consumption was mentioned. The consumption of the maritimes generally is quite low. I have noted a discrepancy in their figures. The minister has stated on previous occasions that the maritimes have a consumption of about 15 pounds a year, but the New Brunswick delegation stated in their brief that we have a consumption of up to 35 pounds. I do not know whether that applies only to some cities or whether it is general, but I feel it is important to know who is consuming the fish in Canada.
In Canada generally consumption is about 13 or 14 pounds per year, and much can be done there. Perhaps the minister can comment on that. Of course, the competition maritime fish products meet in the central Canadian markets is tough and always will be tough. We have to fall back on our luxury fish such as oysters, lobsters and the fine maritimes salmon.
We have good codfish, too.

Yes. After the remarks that have been made in a good vein, I must say with regard to the parliamentary restaurant, that there has been a notable upward trend in the quality and quantity of the fish on its menu, and it deserves a great deal of credit for that.

Reference was also made to the biological interest that we have in New Brunswick regarding the fishing industry. I should like to mention the fact that we have a biological station on the east coast at St. Andrews. There is a smaller facility of the fisheries department at Saint John. Recently there have been certain moves and discussions regarding the possible transfer of two departments, I believe, from St. Andrews to Halifax. I appreciate the difficulty the minister has there. I should imagine his experts and those who know what can be accomplished by that concentration have told him that it would be better to move some of the departments to Halifax. I believe he has promised to consider this matter and has said that for the time being these changes will be dropped, but I would suggest to the minister that there is quite a need for biological study in the bay of Fundy. We have the Saltonstall-Kennedy legislation, which I have mentioned. I understand that vessels are being provided out of these funds and are going right into the bay of Fundy itself. It is essential that co-operation should exist, and this interest in the bay of Fundy should be continued.
Then the New Brunswick economic brief dealt with some suggestions which I should like to mention here today for the consideration of the department. First of all it mentioned that our fishing units are small, and there must be a trend toward larger units. That is difficult to accomplish. I understand that there would be difficulties owing to personal connections; but I feel-and I think nearly everybody will agree-that any concentration or centralization is desirable, and the interests of the individuals are probably looked after by the co-operatives and the other small units. In other words we do not have to fear a monopoly in the fishing industry, because these other factors limit any of the dangers of a monopoly.
Conservation has already been dealt with today by the minister himself and by other speakers. In my area there are three species of fish that are worthy of special consideration. The clam has its problems. The green crab is always bothering it; but the new clamdiggers and other inventions will in the future help us to preserve this valuable fish. Lobster is also a delicacy and enjoys quite a good market, but there are many problems connected with it. The lobster industry now has the new steel traps which are a hope for the future.
Conservation measures in the lobster industry are very controversial. I understand that a member of the department recently said, and I was quite pleased to hear him 67509-112
Supply-Fisheries
speak out, that the closures in the season have not been proved definitely of value, and there is certainly more room for experimentation there.
As the minister said, the salmon constitute our greatest challenge, and I think he meant that particularly with reference to the east coast because we are faced with a tremendous problem there. I am not sure of my information, but I read a while ago that the New Brunswick regional supervisor had retired and I understand that his replacement still remains in Halifax. While I realize that he may be just as capable an individual, we feel that an on the spot, experienced man who could give attention to the particular requirements of the salmon industry would be desirable.
Having said that much about salmon, I simply wish to say that I believe a strong decision by the department, tough as it may be, is necessary. We are coming to the day when somebody has to be hurt in the protection of our salmon interests down there and, as I say, a strong stand is necessary based on what the experts feel is best for the future of that industry. Otherwise we will just be like any other area that becomes industrialized. It will be the end of the salmon. I read the other day that the Don river in Toronto was once one of the greatest spawning grounds in North America, and I could not help but think that we are really up against time more than anything else as far as the future of this specialized industry is concerned.
Transportation has been mentioned by the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, and again I should like to urge consideration of this matter. It was also mentioned in the New Brunswick brief. We need refrigerated cars and attention to these matters so that the competition we meet in the central market will be lessened and fresh fish will be enabled to go into that and other fields.
These are my thoughts, Mr. Chairman. I believe that the briefs and other information given to the Gordon commission are definitely of interest to us. I know that the department has probably taken considerable note of them, particularly the fisheries research council, and these are our hopes for the future. My own personal thoughts are somewhat the same as those of the previous speaker. I think there are little matters as far as the department is concerned that can be looked into and that research, conservation and other problems can be furthered. What we need in the fisheries field today is a little more stimulation and imagination, which the research committee could give. That would create interest

Supply-Fis heries
throughout Canada, bring about improvement with respect to our salmon, and the future of the fisheries would be secured.
In this connection I should like to say finally that in my opinion the minister's trip to Russia was certainly stimulating and imaginative. While it may have been costly, it was the kind of advertising I mean because everybody was aware that the minister was over there on matters having to do with fishing and whaling, and the trip had its good effects. We are pleased to see the minister in good health, and look forward to discussing in detail the further items of the estimates.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to add to the congratulations that have been showered on the minister. I am sure he has had enough, and at any rate he comes from British Columbia and has merely displayed the ability that we expect from a cabinet minister from British Columbia.
It is interesting to note, Mr. Chairman, that one of the first matters to engage the attention of the first government of Canada was the question of protecting our fisheries from the encroachments of foreign fishermen. I suppose that struggle has gone on to some extent to the present day.
I am glad to take part in this debate because for one thing the Pacific biological station is situated at Departure Bay on the outskirts of Nanaimo, and I should like to pay tribute now to the staff of that station for the excellent work they have been doing.
A very encouraging development lately that I have come across has been the growing appreciation on the part of fishermen of the work of the scientists at the Departure Bay station. It has replaced the former rather sceptical attitude, the attitude of the practical man to the trained professional scientist. That point of view is now changing and I think this is quite largely due to the work of the staff members there. I noted last year that they went to the trouble of establishing a very interesting display at the fall fair in Nanaimo, which attracted a great deal of attention and large crowds. I have also noted the manner in which the staff members have made their services available to various local organizations through lectures on their particular subjects. It is to be hoped that the funds made available to this station will certainly not be decreased and will, if necessary, be increased. As I say, the fact that the fishermen are now realizing the value of the work will give added support to it.
I was relieved and reassured by the statements of the minister with regard to the problem of power versus fish. Whether or
fMr. Bell.]
not there is a final ultimate solution to the problem I do not know. I do not know if anybody does, but I am always rather reluctant to see sources of food supply endangered for any other purpose whatever. One of the first things we have to do is eat, and to destroy a source of food supply for a possible advantage in another field is, I think, a very shortsighted policy. I was relieved to hear the minister say that those who are interested in the development of power have how reached the conclusion that they must adapt their operations to the maintenance of our large fishing industry on the Pacific coast.
There are one or two matters I want to bring to the minister's attention at this point because I can see no other place in the estimates to do it. During his address this morning he mentioned the fact that the department has been encouraging the fishermen to fish in the deep sea waters, the open waters off the shore. I have had quite a number of discussions with fishermen in my constituency on this question. Whether or not the suspicion is well grounded I do not know, but I am reporting it to the minister. Many of them seem to feel that the department is pursuing a policy intended to result in having more of the fishing conducted on the Pacific coast by the newer type higher-powered vessels than has been the case in the past, and that one of the methods by which the department is seeking to encourage offshore fishing is by imposing ever more rigid closure seasons on the inside waters. Many of the gill netters and the trollers feel that they are in effect going to be squeezed out of the industry.
I realize, of course, as the minister does, that there is and always has been this battle of the gears going on, more efficient methods driving out less efficient methods, but on the other hand I think we have to remember what the minister told us this morning, that for many fishermen it is not merely a means of livelihood but a way of life. In that regard I know that many of them feel, whether or not it is justified, that the department's policies are endangering their continuation in that way of life.
I have also heard some complaints with regard to the effect of the beam trawlers on certain species of fish. I have heard definite complaints that they have had a most destructive effect on the ling cod supply in the enclosed waters and also on the ground-fish that my colleague, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, mentioned earlier today; that these deep trawlers are scraping the bottom of every living thing and that much of it is being destroyed. Again, that is a matter on which one would have to have expert evidence. I am reporting these things to the

minister for his consideration because these are complaints that I have heard.
There is another matter which affects not merely the Department of Fisheries but also the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. I am rather glad the minister is in his seat. This matter concerns the fishing rights of Indians on rivers. I met with the council of the Cowichan band of Indians before I came east to Ottawa. They placed before me their complaint in this regard. I may say they were able to back up their claim with documentary evidence in the form of agreements signed many, many years ago, which provided that they were to be permitted to continue using weirs on the river, particularly on the Cowichan river, as had been their custom from time immemorial.
This right was abrogated, but in return they were to have certain other fishing rights which they claim they have not been granted. Many of them feel they would like now to go back to the old weir system. I tried to persuade them that was an impossible policy and would be a contradiction to any proper system of fisheries conservation. I do suggest, however, that these Indians have a legitimate grievance and there should be some compensation paid them for the forfeiture of these ancient rights which have been prescribed in definite agreements.
Those are the matters I particularly wanted to bring to the minister's attention. I was hoping that we might have heard from him, and perhaps we may hear on a later occasion, some information with regard to his inquiries into the fishing industry in Russia. I believe that would be of great interest to us. I realize it has nothing to do with the administration of his department, but I should like to express the hope he will seize the first opportunity to give us some description of the sort of industry he discovered there and his opinion as to whether or not their methods could be adapted to our own fishing industry.

I cannot resist the desire to congratulate the minister on his return and restoration to good health. I am certain that his department still needs a guiding hand. There is a great deal of work to be done for the fishery industry of this country. I am sincerely delighted to see him looking so well.
During his speech this morning the minister referred, as I did on February 21, to this all-important question of power versus fish on fish-producing streams in British Columbia. This problem overshadows all other problems in so far as the fishing industry of British Columbia is concerned. The minister called attention to the value of our salmon fisheries industry, $25 million to $50 million, 67509-112J
Supply-Fisheries
but we are faced with the fact that other industries which will be developed from the power produced on our rivers exceed that amount by many, many times.
As I pointed out previously, only a very small proportion of the horsepower which is available in British Columbia is at present being utilized. There are power-hungry industries crying out and straining every nerve to find additional sources of power. Now, we can either sit down and do nothing about this, or else inaugurate a very active and vigorous program to find out how to pass the fish up and down stream over, around or through these various obstacles. There are diverters with which experiments are being conducted; there are different types of spillways, fishways and so forth. However, the problem has not so far been solved. Whether it is by light, electricity, sound or scent, a solution must be found and we cannot take half measures.
I do not think any reasonable amount of money expended in the search for a solution will be money wasted. Of course we are pleased to hear of the very generous donations which have been made to the University of British Columbia by industry to assist the federal government and the universities in finding the answer to this problem. But again, the federal government cannot sit back and leave it entirely to industry to solve the problem. I believe that under the Fisheries Act the minister has certain powers. Well, it is not the use of prohibitive powers we want, it is positive work that we must have. Having referred to this matter previously, I do not intend to pursue that subject any longer. Again I stress that it is the most important of all the problems with which we are faced.
The minister referred to the closure of San Juan strait, and that is a very serious problem for the fishermen of my constituency on Vancouver island. The fishermen from Vancouver island have been following the policy which the government suggested and have been operating farther and farther out to sea, thereby catching a better quality of fish. Now, why should we surrender that advantage? At first we thought we would have to surrender the right to fish on the Canadian side and have only fishing on the American side. I am glad that has been adjusted. I do not see why the right to catch the best quality of fish should be given up in order that second rate fish may be caught in the straits of Georgia or elsewhere. Surely some other form of conservation could be used. I am quite certain that the fishermen of

Supply

Fisheries
Vancouver island are just as anxious to conserve the fish as any other part of the industry, but that they should be asked to carry all the load is something which seems to me unfair.
Then 1 would raise this question. If you are going to put on this closure on the sock-eye, is that going to apply to the other species, the cohoe and the pink? It is extremely difficult to separate those various species because the runs are, in part, simultaneous. A person may be out fishing for pinks and inadvertently catch a spring because the runs overlap. I say, therefore, it is extremely difficult to permit the catching of one type of salmon and prohibit the catching of another type at the same time. I feel that there must be some other way in which conservation can be enforced.
Then I should like to ask whether that is going to apply to the sports fishermen as well. During the fisheries estimates last year I discussed the question of licences. There was an order in council passed which limited the type of individual who could apply for a commercial licence. We are faced with the fact that a good many people take out a licence to supplement their normal means of livelihood by catching fish commercially during a short period of time. They are business and professional men. They take their summer holidays, take out a commercial licence and go fishing. But, then there is the straight sports fisherman. Is he to be barred from fishing in those waters? If so it may have quite a serious effect upon our tourist industry. The attraction of being able to fish during the summertime in those waters brings many people to the district.
When the minister replies I wonder whether he can tell us how many licences were issued last year. According to the order in council which was passed, I believe the licences were limited to Canadian citizens or ex-members of the armed forces, and there had to be a certificate to the effect that they were engaged in catching fish for sale. These were the general qualifications. There were some other exemptions regarding British subjects who had previously been fishing and men who had been helpers.
When the minister replies I wonder whether he can give us information as to the effect of that order in council, whether the number of licences issued has been reduced in any way; whether he has found that there have been any large number of applications from people who were British subjects but not Canadians, and whether the helper clause has been conducive to getting young men to

come and enter the fishing business, sons of fishermen and so forth, which is almost a sort of apprentice class.
There is just one other point I wanted to raise. The minister referred in his final sentence to the question of the pay which fishermen receive. He called attention to the fact that fishermen were one of the more poorly paid classes of people. I am going to be unkind for a moment; I am going to tell him to look at the mote in his own eye, because his fishery officers are the poorest paid officers in any of the departments. I happen to know some of these young men who are acting as fishery officers in British Columbia. I know they are extremely conscientious and hard-working. They are out in all kinds of weather and under circumstances which are quite trying, on account of the fact that often they have to get wet, and go through the bush and up and down the streams at all times of the year, sometimes in very severe weather.
I want to call the minister's attention to these figures which I jotted down this morning. I have taken only one of the junior grades, grade III fishery officer. His salary ranges from $3,870 to $4,260. A grade III commissioner in the civil service starts at $4,290. In the Department of Citizenship and Immigration a grade III officer runs from $4,750 to $5,500; whereas a grade III field officer in the Department of Agriculture, which is somewhat similar, starts at $4,110 and goes up to $4,500, and in another branch of the same department from $4,170 to $4,920.
Perhaps the minister would take that up with the civil service commission. I bring to his attention the fact that his own officers are poorly paid. I know they do good work. I speak feelingly in connection with that. Perhaps if he can bring his field officers in line with the field officers of similar grades in other services it might stimulate an increase all through the industry. We have to raise the standard of the fisheries department and the fishery industry, and not have it regarded as a depressed and poorly paid industry. We cannot make progress if we continue to accept that condition.
In his remarks the minister did not give us the conclusion which had been reached in connection with the prolonged meetings which have been going on in Washington or New York regarding the fur seal. We do not seem to have received any answer. I am glad that after all these years it is now recognized that there are others who feel that perhaps there are too many fur seals. I called attention to that some years ago and I did not get very favourable response. I am pleased that this has been noted.

Then, of course, there is the age old question of the 3-mile limit. We want that settled as far as Hecate straits and the waters around the Queen Charlotte islands are concerned. We are told again that there have been commissions sitting on it. We would like to hear the results of the commissions' work rather than the mere fact that they are sitting. We have been told that they have been sitting for at least three years. Surely they must have reached some conclusion.

Mr. Chairman, rather than repeat what has been said to the Minister of Fisheries I will just tell him what one of the fishermen said to me when he heard of his accident which took place in Russia, as you know, last summer. He said to me, "Tell him that just at the time when at last we really have someone who is more interested in fisheries than any other minister we ever had-" and I will leave out a few other words- "they have ruined our chances forever". I think that expresses pretty well the feelings of the fishermen of the area, and certainly it expresses the feelings of the members of the house who have spoken today.
I should like to draw the attention of the committee to one fact, and I do it particularly for the benefit of some of my fellow Nova Scotians who, because of their innate modesty-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Hear, hear.

-rather hesitate-I am referring to other Nova Scotians-to refer to the amount of fish that is caught in their province or in their constituencies, or the value of the fish. But thanks to a question put on the order paper by the hon. member for Halifax it was drawn to the attention of the house that in the western part of Nova Scotia, in the constituency of Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare, the constituency in fact which my friend who just made the interjection is very proud of-I understand that although he did not have the honour of being born there his ancestors came from there-more fish are landed than in any other constituency in Nova Scotia, and their landed value in dollars is greater than in any other constituency in Nova Scotia. I thank the hon. member for Halifax for having brought that to the attention of the house.
There are three or four items I should like to mention, which have been mentioned by the Minister of Fisheries. I do not intend to speak at any length, but I would like to mention first of all to what our fishermen generally refer to as the insurance plan, but
Supply-Fisheries which I notice the Department of Fisheries refers to as the indemnity plan. They can call it what they like. As far as we are concerned it is an excellent plan, and our people were most appreciative when it was established. It has been very successful as far as I can find out on both coasts, and particularly in my own area in so far as insurance on vessels and boats is concerned, but it has not been so successful in so far as insurance or indemnity on lobster traps is concerned.
I have talked to a great many fishermen. Many of them have taken advantage of it and they have spoken to others about it, but there still seems to be a certain group of fishermen who do not wish to take advantage of such an indemnity plan although I do not understand why. It is an excellent plan, the rates are not high and the protection is worth a great deal. Perhaps the greatest evidence we had of that was at the time of the hurricane in September, 1954, when so many boats were damaged and so many traps lost.
I should like to say to the minister that by and large even those who have not taken advantage of this plan think it is a good one, uud I do hope that as time goes on more fishermen will take advantage of this plan.
When the minister brought into the house his bill for fisheries improvement loans he mentioned that it was impossible to do this until such time as such an insurance or indemnity plan had been established. I realize that this bill which was only introduced last June has not been in effect long enough for us to be certain what its effect will be, but here again the reports are most favourable and I hope when the minister replies to the various questions and comments that have been made he will give us some idea of how many fishermen have taken advantage of this act, and what loans have been made. Perhaps he will say whether or not he feels, as we in our area do, that its success is assured and that over a period of two or three years it will mean to the fishermen what the Farm Improvement Loans Act has meant to the farmer after the first two or three years of its operation.
So far as the salt fish rebate is concerned I am very much inclined to agree with the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo. I think the plan has been a good one. I know that our fishermen object to some of the forms that have to be filled in-perhaps I should say the forms which have to be completed-but I have never seen anyone who has a form to complete who has not felt that the form was too long and too complicated. The main point, however, is that the idea was good and

Supply-Fisheries
it may well be that there will be a different percentage for the light cured fish.
The question concerning territorial waters, which I have mentioned on several occasions, has been mentioned two or three times today.
I do not know that any answer can be given at the present time, but I have done quite a bit of reading on the matter and I must confess that the more I read the more I realize the complications in the problem. I liked the phrase which I read in one of the fisheries bulletins which went something like this: "The legal position in relation to the breadth of territorial waters therefore remains unsatisfactory." I cannot think of a nicer way of expressing what has been the cause of a great disturbance to all of us over a period of years with reference to the 3-mile limit and the 12-mile limit and the bit of water between the 3-mile limit and the 12-mile limit which our trawlers cannot make use of but which United States trawlers can. It is some satisfaction to all of us to know that the matter is being studied, that the Curtis commission has reported that the international law commission recognizes that the practice is not uniform throughout the world, and that some attempt is being made to meet what is a difficult situation.
May I say to the minister that in my constituency there are three or four fish firms that have taken advantage of the bait freezer assistance. They think the plan is an excellent one, and I should like to see more of the smaller fishing plants in the smaller communities take advantage of such a plan. I think they would do so if they realized the amount of good that such a plan can accomplish, the number of fishermen who could make use of it and not have to travel 8, 12 or 15 miles by road or water in order to get their bait. I think there must be some way of simplifying the procedure through which we must go in order to obtain assistance for the establishment of a bait freezer. Perhaps I should not say the procedure should be simplified; I perhaps should have said that it needs to be expedited.
In talking with the fishermen at home during the last few months I have found that more and more they are becoming keenly interested in the protection service, particularly with reference to lobsters. Suggestions are being made by those in the fishing business, as well as the fishermen themselves, that this should be done and that it should be done in order to protect the lobster fisheries and in order to give a greater yield over a period of years.
Not long ago the Minister of Fisheries made an announcement concerning restrictions on the mesh size of the trawl fishing nets, and

it has met with general approval. 1 think over a period of years conservation and protection have been meeting with general approval; and what is more important than anything else, it is meeting with the approval of those who are directly concerned, that is those who are actually doing the fishing themselves.
In conversation with members of the Department of Fisheries and with the minister himself over a period of two or three years, I have pointed out to this department that it is felt on our coast where we have the largest number of small-boat fishermen of any area in Nova Scotia, that we should have at least one larger fishery patrol vessel. I know there is one fairly large vessel which covers all the coast. We have all the smaller vessels and there is no question about the work that is being done by them; but the fishermen feel, particularly at the western end of Nova Scotia, that if we could have one large vessel 125 feet long which could be used more or less as a mother vessel along with the smaller boats in that area, and which could be used in times of emergency when the small fishing boats are broken down, it would be much more effective.
At the present moment it is difficult for the 65-foot patrol boats to get out in very bad weather, and that does seem to be the time when the fishing boats break down. When we look for a navy vessel or a transport vessel they are always so far away from the scene of the emergency that they do not prove very successful at the particular time. I am suggesting that our present plan of air-sea rescue could be improved greatly if we were to have one, two or three 120-foot or 125-foot patrol boats. I think I made it quite clear when speaking directly to the Minister of Fisheries that the people of western Nova Scotia are sure that when he makes that move he will find the most advantageous place for one of these larger vessels will be at the southwestern end of Nova Scotia.
I might ask the minister, while I am directing questions particularly to him, if he will give the house some idea of the success of the metal lobster traps with which the department has been experimenting in my own constituency.
I do not think even these few remarks, Mr. Chairman, should end without making reference to the fact that the Department of Fisheries is always in close touch with the Department of Public Works and the Department of Transport to find out from those departments and from the fishermen themselves their actual needs. For example, we can give assistance in protection and in marketing; we can give assistance and advice in

so far as the construction of boats is concerned, but all that is of little value to us if we do not have the proper wharves and breakwaters and the necessary dredging done in order that the fishermen can set out from those piers and wharves in order to get their catch. The same applies to the Department of Transport, which is concerned with channel marking, lights, fog alarms and so on.
I must say with due appreciation that all the officials of the departments I have just mentioned with whom I have been in contact have not only been most interested in their jobs but have been most courteous. I find in talking with the fishermen that they too appreciate the attitude of these departments. I do not think there is any better evidence of that than the attitude which is apparent from the top of the department right down to the lowest echelon. We hope that same forward looking policy which has been so much in evidence in the last few years will continue during the next few years.

Mr. Chairman, first I should like to congratulate the minister upon being back safely, and hope that he will have good health from now on. I spoke to him when he came back but in case anyone should think I was missing him I do so again.
Perhaps I have no place in a discussion about fish because the fisheries in Manitoba are run by the Manitoba government, but I have always been greatly interested in fishing. I can remember back in 1900 or 1901 when I went out with fishermen on the Firth of Clyde fishing for herring, and I have never lost that desire to go out in a boat every chance I get.
I think the minister knows what I am going to talk about. I have always been interested in the co-operative fund which I know has been a boon and blessing to a lot of fishermen. I have made a visit or two to the east coast and I know the wonderful job that is being done. I notice there is an item in the estimates of $10,000 for British Columbia. I do not begrudge that in the least, but I would like to see some of this education being made available to the fishermen of the prairie provinces. It would be a wonderful thing if arrangements could be made to provide some of these educational facilities, because I know they would make good use of them.
I understood from the minister last year that fishermen's loans are now available to the fishermen of the prairie provinces. When the minister closes this debate I hope he will tell us about the indemnity fund. I know that would be a boon to the fishermen on lake
Supply-Fisheries
Winnipeg and lake Manitoba. It would be a great help to them if they could have insurance for their boats. As a rule fishermen are not great on insurance, and they have never had the opportunity of getting cheap insurance. I do not know whether this comes from the department, but I presume it would come out of the consolidated revenue fund. I should like to see this extended to the prairies. I believe the problem last year was lack of staff but perhaps that can be overcome.
When the minister rises to speak would he tell us what progress is being made with the film that was being prepared on the northern lakes, where fishing conditions are similar to those on lake Winnipeg. Has the film been completed and will it be available this summer or fall for exhibition purposes?
I may say something more on the particular items, but will conclude now by congratulating the minister upon the paper he and his officials are putting out. It is a good paper, and it is an economical paper because it is printed on both sides.
