Mr. Chairman, I wish to avail myself of this opportunity to speak of an increasingly serious condition, the disappearance of salmon from our rivers, like the Restigouche and its tributaries, along the shores of New Brunswick. Salmon is deserting our rivers and the federal government is not doing anything to remedy the situation. In this case, as in so many instances, it prefers to remain inactive.
I simply ask the government to launch an immediate investigation to determine what steps could be taken to restock the rivers of eastern Canada with salmon.
I also ask the government to take at once whatever means may be necessary to remedy the situation as a result of the inquiry.
Admittedly, past investigations into the economic development of the maritimes were followed by practical and helpful recommendations. There can be no doubt that if the federal government had acted upon the recommendations made as a result of such investigations, people in the maritimes would no longer suffer from the chronic economic depression which is driving our young men away from home and which compels too many of our citizens to live in an unbelievable and pitiable state of poverty unknown elsewhere in the country.
I ask that the investigation into the disappearance of salmon from our shores and

Supply-Fisheries
rivers be made with the firm intent to implement without delay resulting recommendations.
Moreover, why is the government penalizing our fishermen, like our farmers and farmhands, by depriving them of the benefits of unemployment insurance? Would the government deny that our fishermen, farmers and bushworkers are among the hardest working people in this country? From early morning until late at night, they spare no effort. The government agrees with that, but has neither the courage nor enough sense of duty to give justice to our fishermen and to our farmers, by extending to them the benefits of unemployment insurance. I urge the government to be fair, honest and loyal towards our fishermen, our farmers and their employees by making them eligible for unemployment insurance benefits.
I also ask the Department of Fisheries to put an end to its policy of discrimination as far as the restocking of lakes and rivers is concerned. I can prove that our good liberals have no trouble at all getting their lakes restocked with trout at no cost while any other group or person has to pay for that service.
I have given the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) some striking examples of that. I simply ask that the restocking of all our lakes, private and otherwise, and of all our rivers, with trout and other fish be carried out at no cost to the owners.
I also ask that a fishway be constructed at Grand Falls to allow the salmon and other fish to go up the Saint John river, which separates the United States and Canada. We all agree that the project would allow salmon to make their way to the top of Grand Falls. The minister himself, in a letter to me, apprized me of the fact that it would only be a matter of stocking the upper reaches of the Saint John river to ensure that the salmon would make their way up the river through this fishway.
I would also ask that a fish-breeding station be established immediately at St. Leonard, New Brunswick, to ensure the restocking of the lakes and rivers in Mada-waska.
I hope that the Minister of Fisheries, now that his health is improved, may be able to look after the affairs of his department more actively. I was deeply concerned by the most unfortunate mishap he had during his trip in Russia.
I invite him to make a tour, or even several tours, in my province to see for himself the pitiable and inexcusable condi-

tions his department tolerates in the northern part of New Brunswick.
(Text);
I do not wish to repeat in English what I have just said in French, save to bring to the attention of the house that our once great salmon fishing industry in our northern New Brunswick rivers is fast disappearing. I request that an immediate survey be made to determine the causes of the disappearance of our salmon, and I request that the recommendations resulting from this survey be implemented without delay.
In regard to salmon fishing, as in regard to almost everything else in the maritimes, we have been treated with the customary indifference, indolence and apathy so characteristic of the federal government. I ask the government to wake up and recognize the seriousness of this problem, which demands immediate attention and action.
For many a year the salmon fishing seasons on our famous rivers, such as the Restigouche, the Upsalquitch, the Kedgwick, were times of great activity and employment. All these rivers are heavy-laden with tradition, story and song. Many of our professional guides on these rivers enjoy international reputations. These famous rivers have played host to great anglers from all corners of the world. This once great sporting industry faces utter ruin unless action is taken, and taken now.
In this instance, as in so many others, such as in the development of hydroelectric power in New Brunswick, such as in the long overdue restoration of our confederation-guaranteed preferential freight rates, which have been permitted to rise 98 per cent since 1947, as in the building of the Chignecto canal, and as in so many other things, the government gives the impression that it considers us in the maritime provinces to be merely so many people in the way and that it would be happy to be rid of us.
What nonsense!
Only some people.

Let me say this. We are a part of Canada and we will be treated as Canadians. I say again and again and again, give us a square deal or quit. If this government cannot help us in regard to this particular problem, then let it stand aside and let us pass, to claim the heritage for our people that this great country can and will provide, just as soon as we have replaced this tired, old, weary government with the type of progressive government which only the Conservative party can provide.

I only have a few moments. I have listened to the tirade from the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska, who blames this government for almost everything. When we came into confederation a certain gentleman who was very prominent here in Ottawa said to me, "I hope you do not make the same mistake those in the mari-times make who for the past 80 years, since they joined confederation, have been grousing about it."
They did not join confederation-

May I say to the hon. member that, if he and the people of the maritimes show a little more energy themselves, probably they will get the treatment from Ottawa that they deserve.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it five o'clock?

The company has spent $125 million on building that railroad and another amount of $125 million on different facilities for the

speechtext:
The records of the house will show that in 1947, when the first bill was passed to permit the present company to build a railroad from Seven Islands through to Knob Lake I took objection to it on second reading. My objection was that the development of the natural resources of this country is contingent upon transportation, and as we had already decided to farm out the iron ore resources of part of Newfoundland and the Ungava region to companies largely controlled in the United States I figured at that time that the government of Canada should at least have the Canadian National Railways build the transportation line from Seven Islands up to where it is today around Knob Lake or Schefferville.
In the past our experience has been that while capital can be found by private companies to go into an area where there are natural resources to be exploited, the history of the Canadian National Railways shows very clearly that once the resource is exploited and there is no longer sufficient remuneration for the railroad to show a substantial profit, the squeeze is then on for Canadian National Railways to take over and maintain the service. We have loaded down that system with debt for a good many years, with the result that it was pretty well ham-[Mr. Brisson.l
strung until the government stepped in and accepted the responsibility. The unfortunate part of the whole thing is that when we have to take over a railroad we take over the bonds at par and assume all the financial responsibility as if it was a going concern, rather than letting it go into liquidation in the way that any other legitimate business would be treated in the event of bankruptcy.
Once you establish a railroad it has to be maintained. Service has to be given to the public whether it is profitable or otherwise to do so. The iron ore deposits are a wasting resource. All mining operations are. The ore is taken out and sooner or later the resource is depleted. If this should be the only industry or resource in the area and the time should come that the railroad is no longer profitable, then the C.N.R. will be saddled with its operation.
Part of the road has already been built. Some 355 miles have been completed and put in operation. Iron ore is being taken out, and the railroad is performing the service for which it was intended. But there are still 300 miles of the line to be completed from Knob lake to Ungava bay. Some $123 million has been spent already in developing the line that has been completed and it would appear that it will take that much, if not more, to complete the rest.
Of course exploration has not been completed in the area that the road under consideration now will serve, and no one is sure exactly what will be found. Nevertheless these people want to proceed with the line. In view of the fact that the company already has over 300 miles of line, some considerable mileage of which is in Quebec and some in Labrador, I think the government should still consider while we are discussing the principle of this bill if we should not retain some rights for the Canadian people in that area.
The iron ore deposits are in the hands of United States companies. I have talked to people who have been in the area, and these companies are doing as they like with respect to the maintenance of towns and so forth. In my opinion the future of the North American continent is based on steel, and the sections of this continent that have the basic steel industries in their hands for the foreseeable future are the people who are going to run this North American continent.
Today the Canadian people have not any stake in that part of the country. In view of the fact that 355 miles of that line are owned by United States companies and the whole resource so far as iron ore deposits are concerned is in the hands of United States companies, I think this government should consider the possibility of having the Canadian National Railways complete that end

of the line so as to retain something in that area in the right of the Canadian people.
I am surprised from time to time to hear members of this house, particularly Liberal members-and you hear this outside of this house most frequently-state that they would rather see our resources in the hands of outside interests than in the hands of the Canadian government. I would rather see our resources in the hands of the Canadian government than in the hands of United States financiers who have no responsibility in this country and are not answerable to anyone except to the extent that they are answerable through bills similar to this for the exploitation of our resources, building railroads and so forth.
I have told Liberal members, "You would rather see the resources in the hands of people who are not answerable to you." Is it not better to have transportation which is opening up a part of the country, and the resources, in the hands of men like the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Minister of Fisheries, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour, who once every four years have to give an account of their stewardship to the Canadian people. If they are not doing right the people can do something about it. But when you farm out the resources for 10, 15 or 20 years and they are in the hands of people who are not answerable to the people of this country, then in my judgment you are asking for trouble and sooner or later you are going to get it.
I think transportation, as exemplified by the Canadian National Railways today, where management has to come before a committee of this house to give an account of their financial arrangements and their plans for the future, is the proper kind of development in the field of natural resources. Transportation presupposes the development of a certain section of the country. I think the section of the country about which we are now talking is going to be a very important section. We are pushing into one of our last frontiers in that particular area. I believe at least 50 per cent of the capital invested in the development of the resources and in the construction of the railway should be held by the government of this country, through the Bank of Canada, in the right of the Canadian people. Then the Canadian people would be in a position legally to talk to those to whom we farm out our resources.
I do not intend to belabour this point, because I have put it on the record time and time again. I do feel that before the bill about which we are now talking passes, perhaps some consideration should be given by the house to the advisability of the government having the Canadian National Railways 67509-113J

develop that new area that has not been explored as yet. Then we would at least hold a transportation line in that 300 miles in the right of the Canadian people.

He said: This is a bill, Mr. Speaker, to incorporate Hydrocarbons Pipeline Limited. There is nothing unusual about it. It follows the usual form of bills that have been introduced and passed from time to time in recent years having to do with the transportation of oil or gas in pipe lines. All the first directors of the company are residents of the city of Winnipeg. The head office of the new company will be in Calgary. When the bill is passed the company will come under the provisions of the Pipe Lines Act. This is being promoted by Canadians. Hydrocarbons Limited was incorporated in 1955 by letters patent under the dominion Companies Act.
At the moment this company, that is Canadian Hydrocarbons Limited, is engaged through subsidiaries in the distribution of propane and butane throughout western Canada, and in western Ontario. Canadian Hydrocarbons Limited proposes to take a substantial interest in the equity capital of the new company. The new company is to be formed for the purpose of constructing and operating a products pipe line between the province of Alberta and the city of Winnipeg in Manitoba, with a possible extension to the head of the lakes. The products to be transported will be liquid petroleum gas products such as propane and butane, and it is planned that the line will be of 6 to 8 inches in diameter.
I think it might be of interest to hon. members at this point if I outlined the petroleum scale. You have heard many pipe-line bills discussed in recent years, petroleum pipe lines, natural gas pipe lines, and now here is a company which proposes a pipe line with a much smaller gauge and transporting something a little different. At the lower end of the petroleum scale you have asphalt and heavy petroleum, varying in specific gravities up to the lighter petroleum distillate and so on until you get to kerosene. Then lighter still is gasoline with which everyone is familiar. Not many are familiar with the fact that next on the scale from gasoline is naphtha.

Private Bills
Then you come up to the borderline between liquids and gases, in which field are butane and propane. Finally, the top of the scale is dry, natural gas. The heavier petroleum products, of course, occupy the largest share in the scale and they require-I believe the Interprovincial pipe line is somewhat less than 20 inches and Trans-Canada pipe line about which we have heard so much and which will carry natural gas, is supposed to be 30 to 36 inches.
In the early days of the Turner field their production only went down as far as naphtha. There was no true gasoline taken from that field. Later on, about 1930, they struck the lower part of the scale. What came out of the ground there was a wet gas that had to be put through separating machines and the naphtha was separated out. This naphtha, without any further processing, was used in the same way that you would use gasoline. The farmers in Alberta would go to the wells and buy the naphtha which was separated from the wet gas and use it in their tractors. It was pretty hot for automobiles, but many of them used it in their cars. The remainder, which included the products I am speaking of, butane and propane, and the gas, at that time was burned and wasted in that way.
This gas would be let off through a standby pipe that would be probably 5 or 6 feet high and perhaps 3 inches in diameter, and it looked just like a big bunsen burner. That gas flame showed up like a bunsen burner flame. It shot up just about as high as the top of this chamber, and day after day the flames at nearly every well would be burning away and you could see the reflection of those flares in the sky a hundred miles away. That gas was power, and this was a waste of something that was essential to all industry. Fortunately, as time has gone by that waste no longer takes place. All the gas will be transported to the various parts of the country where it will be put to useful work. This bill takes care of the last field, that field that is, depending on the pressure, either gas or liquid.
I am sure all hon. members have seen the bottles of this product that are shipped all over for use in stoves. It can be used as tractor fuel, except that it is a little bulkier and harder to handle than gasoline, but it acts just as a gasoline. It complements the use of natural gas. It also has to be removed from natural gas before the gas can be shipped. It will be removed at the well head, stored and transported by this small-gauge pipe line to Winnipeg and later to the head of the lakes. It is expected that the
TMr. Weaver.]
line will go roughly via Edmonton, North Battleford, Saskatoon, Brandon and Winnipeg.
The investment required for the construction, together with the gathering system and storage facilities, will be between $30 and $35 million, with an additional expenditure of about $20 million for the possible extension of the line from Winnipeg to Fort William. This latter figure also includes the additional storage facilities.
Hon. members can see that when the last products of the wells' production are put to work it will mean a saving to all the gas and oil companies in two ways. It will mean that the producers will be able to get a better price for their products at the well head, and it will also mean that the processing companies, such as the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines, will be able to get natural gas at a better price at the well head and everyone, both producer and consumer, will benefit from it.
As with all other private bills, this bill will automatically be sent to one of the standing committees, in this case the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines. Competent officials of the company will be present to answer any questions of a technical nature that hon. members might wish to pose.

Mr. Speaker, just before this bill passes second reading may I say I appreciate the fact that the hon. gentleman has moved the bill because it is standing in his name today, but it is quite a bill. When I look at the powers to be conferred by this particular bill I find they are exceedingly wide and large.
The house has been asked to adopt the principle of this bill without knowing anything about it. When I say "without knowing anything about it" I mean it is the last bill placed at least on my file. It has been before the gentlemen of the other place; I see it was passed by them on February 29, and it reached here I think today. Probably it was placed on my file this morning, so that one has not had even a chance to read the powers that are conferred. If hon. members will look at the powers they will see that they are very wide, very comprehensive and embrace almost anything that a company could wish to do, including the operation of airfields, the building of towns, the control of real estate, the subdivision of property and every other thing that is conceivable.
Personally, before I give consent to the second reading of this bill, Mr. Speaker, I suggest to the hon. member that we should have an opportunity to look it over. I would

like to read, as a matter of fact, what the mover and the hon. gentlemen in the other place had to say about it. This is a bill that contemplates a $35 million project with the possible expenditure of another $20 million. This $55 million project has been brought in this afternoon without any opportunity for hon. members to read the provisions of the bill or at least study the representations that have been made.
It is true that it goes to a standing committee of the house. That is all right; but once we adopt the principle of the bill we give a certain approval to it. Before we are asked to do that, Mr. Speaker, we should at least have some opportunity of looking into the matter. I therefore move the adjournment of the debate so we may do that.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. R. Balcom (for Mr. Hunter) moved
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 158, for the relief of Lorinc Orvos Nagy.

Mr. Speaker, in support of what has been said by my colleague I might mention that the solicitor for the petitioner seemed to assume that if adultery were established the divorce would be granted automatically. At page 22 of the evidence the petitioner's lawyer had this to say:
What has it got to do with this hearing supposing her husband did beat her, the proper thing to do would have been to take a separation action before the court in Montreal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If they separated by reason of acts of cruelty on his part, it is a ground for us refusing to grant the divorce.
Later on the counsel had this to say:
Supposing he did beat her once and then she left the house in 1954, would that excuse adultery? We are here before this honourable committee on a question of adultery-on a divorce matter, which is granted on adultery being proven, and unless you can prove to us that our man is not coming here with clean hands, well all right.
I understand that this is the first contested case which has come to our attention this year. The principle was established last year that we did not necessarily have to grant a divorce even though adultery was claimed and proved. I think if this wife had been suing for divorce she would have had no trouble in submitting evidence that would have warranted the other house recommending that a divorce be granted, but her lawyer did not come here with that in mind. However, the questions which he asked the petitioner I think would establish in the minds of most fair-minded people that the husband had no business coming to parliament with his sort of record and taking up the time of members of the Senate and of this house in reviewing the evidence which is available to all those who care to read it.
Private Bills
I hope that our colleagues from the province of Quebec will not merely sit out this particular vote but will support the motion for the six months' hoist.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. E. Harris (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am a little surprised that my hon. friends of the opposition seem to have discovered a new principle of law.
What opposition?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: There is only one real opposition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I beg your pardon; that some hon. members of the opposition seem to have discovered a new principle of law which has been drawn to the attention of counsel for the applicant in this case. I listened to the hon. member for Mackenzie read portions of the evidence, and as far as I could follow them I have no quarrel with the statements that were made. There has been more than one case in which adultery has been proved on both sides where a divorce has been granted. Because of the nature of the circumstances the divorce was granted. It may well be that hon. members may object that where there is adultery on both sides there should be no divorce granted no matter what the circumstances may be, but I would point out that that is not necessarily the guiding rule.
From what I have heard this afternoon, there were perhaps some unhappy occasions between the two parties in this particular case regardless of the question of adultery. I was not able to follow the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam in his reference to the $100 a month. I understood him to say that the husband had offered the wife this money to remain in the household but had not paid it to her until she had left the household. I am not too familiar with the nature of the difficulty there.
But let us suppose that this is a case where there has been marital trouble, where in fact the husband may be assumed to have been guilty of adultery himself. There is an undoubted right on the part of parliament to reject the application, and no one quarrels with that. But the point made by the hon. member for Mackenzie is that this man should have his application rejected because he seems to have been guilty of some form of misdemeanor, be it adultery or otherwise.
I think perhaps the hon. member is being a little premature.
Any citizen of Canada has the right to come here with a petition, and we ought to judge that petition on its merits and not on the merits of the petitioner. I think the hon. member will agree with me that that is so. It may well be that a person guilty

Private Bills
of a misdemeanour will petition this parliament in order to establish his rights, and surely my hon. friend would not suggest that because there has been a misdemeanor the petition should be rejected on that ground alone.
For that reason I wonder if the motion has been made with full consideration of what we are supposed to do in the House of Commons. Are we not supposed to pass on the merits of the petition for divorce after consideration in committee? My understanding always has been that the purpose of second reading-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Would the minister permit a question before he leaves that phase of the matter? I understand that from the minister's point of view a person guilty of a misdemeanor may seek certain rights, but is it not so that in this instance the alleged right which the husband seeks would cause suffering so far as the wife is concerned, in that she would be denied certain moneys to which she is now entitled? Do not both sides of the matter have to be considered?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have never understood that in hearing a petition before parliament we would not hear arguments on both sides. If in this case the wife has a certain right with respect to moneys, as has been suggested, that right no doubt would be taken into account by the committee, and probably was taken into account in the other place. If it was not, I suppose it was because it was not presented to them. If I have not made the answer my hon. friend expected I would be glad if he would try to clarify for me what he is trying to suggest.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Apparently the minister has not caught the point I was trying to make. My point is that in granting the request that has been made my hon. friends who have read this case feel that a wrong would be done to the wife. Does not that have to be taken into consideration by the house before we can entertain the minister's argument about granting a person his alleged rights?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I do not suggest that giving second reading here was a decision in favour of the husband with respect to the wife. I do not think anyone has suggested that second reading of the divorce bill does that. In fact I recall that in discussion, the last time we spoke of divorce bills in this house, it was said and repeated, I think, by Mr. Speaker that on second reading what we said in this house was that, assuming that subsequent investigation did in fact establish what was asserted in the petition, then we

might grant third reading to a bill. Perhaps I have not expressed it as elegantly as others might do.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That was an unfinished discussion. It would depend on how far one reads citation 769 in Beauchesne's third edition.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
That may be so, but I have always been given to understand that that is the principle in second reading of private bills brought before the house. If my hon. friend wants to discuss the matter with Mr. Speaker on another occasion, I have no objection to him doing so, but while I have been here I have never thought that I was obliged, after second reading, to approve a private bill in committee, and much less was I committed to giving third reading to it by the mere fact that we had given second reading.
I would not delay the house unduly, but quite apparently the citation does in fact refer to the conditional nature of second reading.
. . . the house, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the bill-
The principle, quite obviously, is that a divorce may be granted. It goes on to say:
-conditionally, and subject to the proof of such allegations before the committee.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Read on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Our concern is over the principle of this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The principle of this bill is to grant a divorce if the facts are proven to the committee. It is not a decision in principle that the divorce should be granted. There is a great deal of difference between the two. I think my hon. friends opposite might sometimes just give a little consideration to whether or not they do oppose all divorce bills. I have heard the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre say "on division" every time we have passed a bill this session and probably on earlier occasions. I have never heard him say in this house that he

was opposed to all divorce. It he is opposed to all divorce, I can understand his action. If he is not opposed to all divorce, I cannot understand it, except on a basis which I would not impute to my hon. friend under any circumstances in this house.
What, never?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I think the minister knows to what I am registering opposition when I oppose individual divorce bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Explain for the benefit of the rest of us.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am sure the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration knows too.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: I do not know.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am sure the Minister of Fisheries knows too.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: I can assure you it is a genuine desire for information on my part.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Could I give my hon. friend the opportunity merely to answer my question? Is this a matter of principle? Is he by conscience bound to oppose all divorce?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is the minister not capable of talking for another three minutes?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Quite.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, I am capable of speaking a good deal longer, but there is not very much purpose in speaking on this question.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Since the minister is going to speak anyway, perhaps I can make it clear that every time a divorce comes up we are opposed to the principle of parliament dealing with such divorces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
On that point then, Mr. Speaker, I suppose that every member of parliament is entitled to take any view he likes about the British North America Act; that it should not be enforced or it should not be operative in parliament. I take it
Committees of the House Mr. Knowles: I am helping the minister out, because there are only two minutes left.
They are both breaking the rules.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Is the minister not aware
that other lawyers believe that the provision in the British North America Act providing that parliament would make general rules concerning divorce was made with no notion that we would be handling individual divorce cases?

I rise on a point of order. I understand that you, Mr. Speaker, are in the chair and we are not in the committee of supply. The hon. gentlemen who have been speaking have been talking back and forth to each other and not addressing the Chair at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I apologize at once, Mr. Speaker. I agree with my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre that there have been two views taken of that section of the British North America Act. I suppose that as a so-called reformer he would like to undo in 1956 something that parliament has been doing for a number of years, just on the general principle that what has been is wrong and therefore it can be improved upon by something he might devise.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is my hon. friend, as a Liberal, opposed to reform?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As a Liberal, I am confident that the Liberal party over the years has been the party of reform and the only effective party of reform in this country.
You deceive yourself.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I take this opportunity of saying that I agreed with the point of order raised by the hon. member for Trinity-Conception (Mr. Stick). I also hope that the discussion of the last five or ten minutes will not be taken as a precedent as to relevancy on the second reading of a particular divorce bill.
that my hon. friend-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Does the minister interpret the British North America Act in that respect as having anticipated that parliament would deal with individual divorces?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have not the slightest doubt in the world that that was the thought because, from the day I started practising law, I came here to speak for divorces in the other place, when we had no divorce jurisdiction in the province of Ontario.
